Background

Radiation-induced cavernous malformation (CM) and chronic encapsulated intracerebral hematoma (CEIH) are rare but well-described long-term sequelae of radiotherapy. The authors report a case of an intracranial dural arteriovenous fistula (DAVF) that was treated with conventional radiotherapy and subsequently developed these uncommon lesions in chronological order.

Observations

A 52-year-old woman with a left transverse-sigmoid sinus DAVF underwent traditional radiotherapy at another institution. Following treatment, she developed disabling vertigo. Serial imaging surveillance revealed radiation-induced changes (RICs) in the cerebellum 2 years posttreatment. A de novo CM subsequently emerged within the center of the RIC after a latent period of approximately 3 years. Owing to persistent symptoms, the patient underwent left retrosigmoid craniotomy 4 years after radiotherapy. Although vertigo improved significantly postoperatively, she developed progressive visual impairment 4 years later. Follow-up MRI demonstrated an encapsulated hematoma in the left occipital region within the prior radiation field. A second craniotomy was performed, and histopathological examination confirmed CEIH.

Lessons

This illustrative case underscores the importance of appropriate treatment selection and highlights the potential for significant adverse effects associated with suboptimal radiotherapy planning. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26598.

title: Primary cauda equina neuroendocrine tumor mimicking myxopapillary ependymoma: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Primary cauda equina neuroendocrine tumors (CENETs) are rare intradural extramedullary neoplasms that were historically termed cauda equina paragangliomas. They may resemble more common cauda equina lesions, including myxopapillary ependymoma and schwannoma, on preoperative imaging. Recent molecular and immunohistochemical studies support CENET as a distinct entity, creating a need for practical diagnostic frameworks that separate primary tumors from metastatic neuroendocrine disease and nonneuroendocrine mimics. Observations A 42-year-old woman presented with progressive nocturnal low back pain, bilateral leg heaviness, lower extremity numbness, and urinary incontinence. MRI demonstrated a 5-cm L1-3 intradural extramedullary mass nearly occupying the spinal canal, with cauda equina compression and prominent surrounding vessels. She underwent urgent L1-3 laminoplasty and microsurgical resection. Intraoperatively, the tumor was extremely vascular, friable, and associated with the filum terminale. Gross-total resection was achieved. Pathology demonstrated a WHO grade 1 primary CENET with neuroendocrine marker expression, CK8/18 positivity, low proliferative index, and no evidence of systemic neuroendocrine malignancy on postoperative staging. Lessons Cauda equina neuroendocrine lesions should be approached as a diagnostic spectrum. Clinical tempo, lesion multiplicity, imaging clues, intraoperative vascularity, and immunohistochemical/molecular workup can help distinguish primary CENET from metastatic neuroendocrine disease and mimics. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26609.

title: Surgical decompression of uveal melanoma with optic chiasmal extension via a modified orbitozygomatic approach: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Uveal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of adulthood. Perineural spread along the optic nerve to the optic chiasm is exceedingly rare, with only 4 previously published cases. No standard neurosurgical management has been established. Observations A 65-year-old woman presented with progressive right-sided monocular vision loss over 1 year, subsequently developing left temporal hemianopia. MRI demonstrated a 3.3 × 2.9 × 2.2-cm right intraconal mass extending through the orbital apex along the optic nerve to the optic chiasm, with a 2.8 × 1.9 × 1.5-cm suprasellar component. A right modified one-piece orbitozygomatic craniotomy achieved subtotal resection of the suprasellar disease and decompressed the contralateral optic nerve. The patient received combination ipilimumab/nivolumab, 60 Gy in 30 fractions adjuvant orbital radiotherapy, nivolumab/relatlimab (progression), 27 Gy in 3 fractions stereotactic radiosurgery for new intracranial metastases, and salvage temozolomide with bevacizumab. She remained alive with stable disease at 12 months. Lessons To the authors' knowledge, this is the first reported case of uveal melanoma with optic chiasmal extension managed by a modified orbitozygomatic approach. Contralateral visual field deficits in a patient with an ipsilateral orbital mass should prompt dedicated cranial imaging. Multidisciplinary care can achieve meaningful disease control even when first-line immunotherapies fail. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26734.

title: First reported case of intradural extramedullary epithelioid hemangioma of the cauda equina: resection of an extremely rare vascular neoplasm. Illustrative case.
abstract: Background Intradural extramedullary (IDEM) tumors of the cauda equina are most often meningiomas, nerve sheath tumors, and myxopapillary ependymomas; purely vascular IDEM lesions are exceptionally rare. Fewer than 30 IDEM hemangiomas have been reported, mostly cavernous or capillary. Epithelioid hemangioma (EH), a benign vascular neoplasm arising in soft tissue and bone, has not previously been reported at the cauda equina. Observations A 63-year-old male with prior cutaneous melanoma presented with 3 months of progressive left L5-distribution radicular pain. MRI showed a 1.0 × 2.0-cm well-circumscribed IDEM mass at L4-5 with left L5-S1 foraminal stenosis. Under intraoperative ultrasound localization and continuous multimodal neurophysiological monitoring, en bloc gross-total resection was achieved through L4-5 laminectomy. Histopathological analysis revealed a well-circumscribed vascular neoplasm with lobular endothelial architecture and no cytological atypia; immunohistochemical analysis (ERG, CD31, and CD34 positivity; HHV8, inhibin, and melanocytic marker negativity) established the diagnosis of EH. At the 7-week follow-up, gross-total resection was confirmed on postoperative MRI. Lessons To the authors' knowledge, this is the first reported intradural EH at any spinal level. Recognition of epithelioid endothelial morphology combined with a comprehensive vascular and melanocytic immunohistochemistry panel is essential for diagnosis and separates EH from more common intradural vascular differentials. https://thejns.org/doi/abs/10.3171/CASE26857.

title: Quantifying "Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus"-like Brain Morphometry patterns in an Alzheimer's Disease Cohort.
abstract: Background and purpose Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is largely underdiagnosed. It is a potentially treatable contributor to cognitive decline, and cognitive improvement may occur even with comorbid Alzheimer's disease. However, iNPH-related imaging features can overlap with age-related and neurodegenerative atrophy, making differentiation difficult. Automated morphometric profiling of NPH-like patterns in biomarker-defined Alzheimer's disease cohorts has not been systematically explored. This pilot study aimed to quantify iNPH-like brain morphometry in an Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort using deep-learning-based morphometry and automated callosal angle measurement. Materials and methods We included N=30 amyloid-negative reference iNPH patients and N=1003 ADNI participants with structural T1-weighted MRI and CSF biomarkers. Age- and sex-adjusted volumetric z-scores were obtained using a deep-learning-based morphometry algorithm. We derived an iNPH morphometric profile using principal component analysis and Gaussian modeling of the reference iNPH cohort and applied it to the ADNI participants to compute individual iNPH similarity scores. We also automated callosal angle measurement for further clinical representation. We compared scores across cognitive stages and biological Alzheimer's disease groups and evaluated against expert Radscale review. Results iNPH-like morphometry increased with cognitive impairment, with mean differences of 0.03 between cognitively normal and mild cognitive impairment (p=0.06), 0.06 between mild cognitive impairment and dementia (p<0.001), and 0.09 between cognitively normal and dementia groups (p<0.001). Among cognitively impaired participants, scores were higher in biologically-defined Alzheimer's disease patients than biologically-defined non-Alzheimer's disease patients (mean difference=0.08, p<0.001). The iNPH similarity score correlated most strongly with ventricular enlargement features. Automated callosal angle measurements showed high agreement with expert ratings (Gwet's AC1 = 0.939) and angles below 90° occurred in 1.5% of ADNI participants. Conclusions Automated normative morphometric profiling and callosal angle quantification identified heterogeneous iNPH-like structural patterns in the ADNI cohort. These tools provide a scalable approach for characterizing iNPH-like imaging features in dementia cohorts where identifying a potentially treatable contributor to cognitive impairment remains relevant. Further clinical validation remains necessary.

title: Venous Outflow Imaging in Acute Ischemic Stroke: An ASFNR State of Practice.
abstract: Background Venous outflow (VO) imaging describes the egress limb of the cerebral collateral circulation and has been associated with outcome in acute ischemic stroke; its added value beyond arterial collaterals and perfusion measures remains uncertain. More than a dozen VO measures have been proposed on CT and MR techniques used in acute stroke, spanning three physical signals: venous opacification, venous transit and venous oxygenation. They differ in what they measure, in evidence maturity and in readiness for reporting. Methods A writing group reviewed the peer-reviewed studies of cerebral venous drainage measures in acute ischemic stroke. The scope is CT and MRI obtained during routine acute stroke evaluation, excluding measures that require catheter angiography or ultrasound. We describe each measure's acquisition, definition, evidence and technical limitations, and propose a reporting framework based on these features. Key message VO markers are descriptive prognostic measures, not treatment-selection criteria. The cortical vein opacification score (COVES) has the most mature CTA evidence and may be considered when venous timing is adequate, though meta-analyses support an association rather than a threshold; comprehensive venous outflow (CVO) adds the internal cerebral vein. Prolonged venous transit (PVT) adds a temporal dimension read from perfusion, but remains investigational, as do the composite arterial-venous scores, quantitative venous timing and oxygen extraction fraction mapping. Susceptibility signs index deoxygenation and venous blood volume, not drainage. Reporting should name the technique and describe opacification, transit or oxygenation findings in their own terms. The evidence base is predominantly anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion imaged before thrombectomy.
originalAbstract:
Background

Venous outflow (VO) imaging describes the egress limb of the cerebral collateral circulation and has been associated with outcome in acute ischemic stroke; its added value beyond arterial collaterals and perfusion measures remains uncertain. More than a dozen VO measures have been proposed on CT and MR techniques used in acute stroke, spanning three physical signals: venous opacification, venous transit and venous oxygenation. They differ in what they measure, in evidence maturity and in readiness for reporting.

Methods

A writing group reviewed the peer-reviewed studies of cerebral venous drainage measures in acute ischemic stroke. The scope is CT and MRI obtained during routine acute stroke evaluation, excluding measures that require catheter angiography or ultrasound. We describe each measure's acquisition, definition, evidence and technical limitations, and propose a reporting framework based on these features.

Key message

VO markers are descriptive prognostic measures, not treatment-selection criteria. The cortical vein opacification score (COVES) has the most mature CTA evidence and may be considered when venous timing is adequate, though meta-analyses support an association rather than a threshold; comprehensive venous outflow (CVO) adds the internal cerebral vein. Prolonged venous transit (PVT) adds a temporal dimension read from perfusion, but remains investigational, as do the composite arterial-venous scores, quantitative venous timing and oxygen extraction fraction mapping. Susceptibility signs index deoxygenation and venous blood volume, not drainage. Reporting should name the technique and describe opacification, transit or oxygenation findings in their own terms. The evidence base is predominantly anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion imaged before thrombectomy.

title: Deep Learning-Accelerated 3D T2 CUBE MRI of the Cochlea at 1.5T and 3T: Sonic DL With AIR Recon DL Versus AIR Recon DL Alone.
abstract: Background and purpose Three-dimensional fast spin-echo MR cisternography (CUBE) of the internal auditory canal (IAC) and cerebellopontine angle (CPA) requires longer acquisition times that can limit clinical throughput. We evaluated whether a deep learning (DL)-based highly accelerated reconstruction technique, Sonic DL`™ (SDL), combined with a commercially available DL denoising reconstruction (AIR™ Recon DL, ARDL), preserves or improves subjective image quality and cochlear anatomy visualization relative to standard CUBE-ARDL while shortening scan time. Materials and methods Consecutive patients underwent brain MRI for suspected IAC pathology at 1.5T and 3T with paired acquisition of standard 3D CUBE-ARDL and an accelerated 3D CUBE-SDL sequence. Both used the same voxel size at 1.5T (0.6x0.6x1.2 mm 3 ) and 3T (0.6x0.6x0.6 mm 3 ). Scan times for CUBE-ARDL versus CUBE-SDL were 2:33 versus 1:41 min at 1.5T and 1:55 versus 1:11 min at 3T. Two independent neuroradiologists blinded to MRI acquisition method scored randomized, de-identified images on a 5-point Likert scale across five domains (overall image quality, noise, sharpness, artifacts, cochlear anatomy visualization). Reader-averaged scores for CUBE-ARDL and CUBE-SDL were compared with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with reader-specific and cumulative link mixed model (CLMM) sensitivity analyses and false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment; intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) quantified inter-reader reliability for each technique; Gwet's AC2 and weighted (Conger's) kappa with linear ordinal weights quantified pooled inter-reader agreement. Results After exclusion of 5 training cases per field strength, 49 (1.5T) and 34 (3T) patients were analyzed. CUBE-SDL scored significantly better than CUBE-ARDL for all five domains at both field strengths (all FDR-adjusted P < .001), consistently for each reader and in the CLMM. Inter-reader reliability (ICC) for CUBE-SDL was moderate-to-excellent at 3T (0.63-0.92) and moderate at 1.5T (0.65-0.74), generally exceeding CUBE-ARDL (3T: 0.35-0.61; 1.5T: 0.50-0.71). Pooled inter-reader agreement (Gwet's AC2) ranged from 0.56 to 0.89. Conclusions A combined Sonic DL acceleration with ARDL-denoised reconstruction for 3D T2 CUBE produced significantly higher subjective image quality at both 1.5T and 3T, and, at 3T, higher inter-reader reliability than standard CUBE-ARDL, while shortening acquisition time by 34%-38%. These findings support further evaluation, including diagnostic accuracy studies, of CUBE-SDL as an alternative to CUBE-ARDL.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Arterial Spin-Labeling MRI in the Presurgical Evaluation of Focal Epilepsy and the Limits of Current Evidence for Predicting Surgical Outcome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background and purpose Arterial spin-labeling (ASL) MR imaging is a noninvasive perfusion technique used in presurgical evaluation of focal epilepsy. A 2021 meta-analysis assessed its accuracy for identifying perfusion abnormalities concordant with the epileptogenic zone (EZ) but predated later studies and partly derived specificity from healthy-control true negatives. We re-estimated the diagnostic accuracy of ASL for EZ-concordant perfusion abnormalities with explicit handling of true negatives, and tested whether current data permit a quantitative estimate of the relationship between ASL findings and postsurgical seizure freedom. Materials and methods Following PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-DTA, we searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Scopus from inception to June 2026 for English-language primary studies (≥10 patients) of ASL for EZ localization or surgical-outcome evaluation in focal epilepsy. Random-effects models estimated pooled sensitivity (logit; primary), an exploratory specificity, a logit concordance/detection proportion, and a Freeman-Tukey seizure-free proportion. Because true negatives were absent by design, a joint bivariate/HSROC model was not estimable. Risk of bias used QUADAS-2 and QUIPS; certainty of evidence used a DTA-adapted GRADE approach. Results Fifteen studies were included. The primary analysis (8 studies, 160 patients) yielded a pooled ASL sensitivity for EZ-concordant abnormalities of 0.73 (95% CI, 0.65-0.80; I 2 = 0.0%). The concordance/detection proportion was 0.78 (95% CI, 0.62-0.89; 4 studies), and exploratory specificity 0.37 (95% CI, 0.13-0.71; 5 studies). In the surgical-outcome arm, the pooled seizure-free proportion (Engel I/ILAE 1) was 0.68 (95% CI, 0.58-0.77; 4 studies) and 0.71 (95% CI, 0.56-0.84) in a stricter analysis. Critically, a pooled odds ratio for seizure freedom in ASL-concordant versus ASL-discordant resections could not be computed: the required cross-tabulation was reported in no study. Conclusions ASL has moderate, stable sensitivity for identifying perfusion abnormalities concordant with the anatomo-electro-clinically defined EZ, whereas specificity is not estimable from current single-group designs. ASL-linked surgical cohorts achieve seizure freedom in two-thirds of operated patients, but whether ASL-resection concordance predicts seizure freedom is unquantifiable: a reporting gap, not a null result. Until outcome is reported stratified by ASL-resection concordance, ASL should be used as a localizing adjunct, not a prognostic marker.

Until outcome is reported stratified by ASL-resection concordance, ASL should be used as a localizing adjunct, not a prognostic marker.

title: Association Between Tissue No-Reflow and Prognosis After successful Recanalization in Endovascular Treatment of Intracranial Atherosclerotic Occlusion: A Post Hoc Subgroup Analysis of the ANGEL-REBOOT Trial.
abstract: Background No-reflow after successful endovascular treatment (EVT) predicts poor outcomes in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) due to intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (ICAS), but its optimal evaluation and prognostic value remain unclear. This study assessed computed tomography perfusion (CTP)-defined no-reflow for predicting outcomes in ICAS-related large vessel occlusion (ICAS-LVO). Methods This retrospective post hoc analysis included patients from the prospective ANGEL-REBOOT trial with anterior circulation ICAS-LVO, successful eTICI 2b/3 recanalization, and postoperative 24-hour CTP. No-reflow was defined as persistent hypoperfusion (Tmax >4s or >6s) after recanalization. Outcomes included 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score (poor outcome ≥3) and 24-hour National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score. Results In this exploratory post-hoc analysis, the optimal cohort derived cutoff value for Tmax > 4s hypoperfusion volume was 95.8 mL. Among 64 patients, Tmax >4s hypoperfusion volume ≥95.8 mL best predicted poor 90-day outcome (area under the curve [AUC] 0.75). Larger Tmax >4s volumes correlated with worse 90-day mRS scores (P=0.04) and higher 24-hour NIHSS scores (P=0.006). Tmax >6s (cutoff 9.9 mL, AUC 0.690) only predicted higher 24-hour NIHSS score (P=0.001) but not 90-day outcomes (P=0.12). Conclusions Postoperative 24-hour CTP Tmax > 4 s hypoperfusion volume showed a trend toward better prediction of 90-day poor functional outcomes compared with Tmax > 6 s in recanalized ICAS-LVO patients.

title: Half-Dose Gadopiclenol versus Full-Dose Gadobutrol for Hydrops MR Imaging: Comparison in Contralateral Clinically Unaffected Ears.
abstract: Background and purpose Hydrops MR imaging, performed 4 hours after IV gadolinium administration, requires sufficient contrast-agent accumulation in the perilymph to delineate the nonenhancing endolymphatic spaces. The higher relaxivity of gadopiclenol may reduce gadolinium exposure while preserving perilymphatic enhancement and anatomic detail. Clinically unaffected contralateral reference ears provide a standardized reference that minimizes disease-related confounding. We compared half-dose gadopiclenol (0.05 mmol/kg; half the gadolinium dose) with full-dose gadobutrol (0.1 mmol/kg) for hydrops MR imaging. Materials and methods This retrospective study reviewed 90 consecutive patients referred for hydrops MR imaging. Forty-five received gadobutrol (1.0 mmol/mL; 0.1 mmol/kg), and 45 received gadopiclenol (0.5 mmol/mL; 0.05 mmol/kg). Two experienced head and neck radiologists, blinded to clinical findings and contrast agent, independently evaluated the clinically unaffected reference ear. Quantitative endpoints were the signal intensity ratio (SIR) and reference-normalized contrast (RNC); qualitative endpoints were separate delineation of the saccule and utricle and visibility of the 3 semicircular canal ampullae. The prespecified noninferiority margin was 0.5 units, with a sensitivity analysis using 0.25 units. Results Seventy-one patients were included: 37 received gadopiclenol and 34 received gadobutrol. Nineteen were excluded because of motion degradation, suspected bilateral disease, or abnormal audiometric or MR imaging findings in the reference ear. Mean reader-averaged SIR was 8.15 (SD, 1.51) with gadopiclenol and 7.59 (SD, 1.40) with gadobutrol, yielding a mean difference of 0.56 (95% CI, -0.13 to 1.25). Mean reader-averaged RNC was 7.66 (SD, 1.56) and 6.97 (SD, 1.37), respectively, yielding a mean difference of 0.69 (95% CI, 0.00 to 1.39). Both lower confidence limits exceeded the noninferiority boundary of -0.5; noninferiority was maintained using -0.25. Interreader reliability was excellent for SIR (ICC, 0.915; 95% CI, 0.868-0.946) and RNC (ICC, 0.925; 95% CI, 0.882-0.952). Qualitative assessments showed no significant between-group differences. Where estimable, Cohen κ ranged from 0.66 to 1.00; observed agreement was 97.2%-100% for features with nonestimable κ. Conclusions In clinically unaffected reference ears, gadopiclenol at 0.05 mmol/kg provides quantitative perilymphatic enhancement noninferior to that of gadobutrol at 0.1 mmol/kg, with comparable qualitative anatomic delineation. Higher-relaxivity gadopiclenol may therefore reduce gadolinium exposure without compromising reference-ear image quality.

title: ASFNR Clinical State-of-Practice in Neuroimaging of Minor Large Vessel Occlusion Stroke.
abstract: Background Minor ischemic stroke (MIS) with anterior large vessel occlusion (LVO) is a distinct stroke subtype in which mild neurological deficits may mask a substantial volume of threatened but salvageable brain tissue. Despite a baseline NIHSS≤5, nearly one-third of patients experience poor functional outcomes, often due to early neurological deterioration (END). Current evidence and ongoing trials Patients with LVO-MIS were markedly underrepresented in landmark thrombectomy trials, resulting in limited evidence to guide treatment. Retrospective studies have identified imaging biomarkers of END, including proximal occlusion, clot length, collateral status, and perfusion mismatch, but the benefit of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) remains uncertain. Ongoing randomized controlled trials, including STEP and MOSTE, are expected to define the role of EVT and imaging-based patient selection in this population. Purpose To summarize the current state of neuroimaging in anterior circulation LVO-MIS and provide a practical imaging workflow and reporting checklist for diagnosis, prognostication, and treatment selection. Key points CTA remains the primary modality for LVO detection and collateral assessment, while CT and MR perfusion identify salvageable tissue and predict END beyond baseline NIHSS. MRI further refines infarct core, perfusion deficit, and thrombus characterization. Current AI-based LVO detection tools improve stroke triage but require careful human oversight because proximal M2 and non-terminus ICA occlusions may be missed. Conclusion Pending results from ongoing trials, tissue-based imaging with CTA, CT perfusion, and MR perfusion can complement clinical assessment to improve risk stratification and individualized treatment decisions. Advances in quantitative imaging and artificial intelligence are expected to further enable precision imaging-guided management of LVO-MIS.

title: Conformal Uncertainty for Preoperative MRI Radiomic Glioma Subtyping: Showing When the Model Cannot Separate Subtypes.
abstract: MRI radiomic models predict WHO 2021 glioma subtypes with high AUCs, but reporting only the most probable subtype (argmax) can miss the less common oligodendroglioma. We evaluated whether class-conditional conformal prediction, which sets a separate probability cutoff for each subtype, lets a radiomic model return a set of plausible subtypes for each patient before tissue diagnosis, hypothesizing that it would cover all three subtypes at the target rate at the cost of larger sets. We retrospectively analyzed 1544 patients with preoperative T1, T2, contrast-enhanced T1, and FLAIR MRI from four public datasets. A random forest trained on TCGA and UCSF-PDGM (n=611) was applied unchanged to the Erasmus Glioma Database (EGD, n=404) and UTSW-Glioma (n=529), each split 200 times into a calibration half, used to fit every rule, and a test half. Class-conditional conformal prediction was compared with single-subtype rules, probability sets, abstention, and standard conformal prediction (one shared cutoff). Rules were compared on per-subtype coverage (the share of patients whose set contained the true subtype), mean set size, and the share of patients given a single subtype and its accuracy. Per-subtype AUCs were 0.87-0.96 (EGD) and 0.82-0.91 (UTSW-Glioma), yet argmax identified 7 of 73 and 4 of 63 oligodendrogliomas. At the 90% target, only class-conditional conformal prediction reached it for all three subtypes in both cohorts (mean coverage 0.90-0.93, mean set size 1.39 and 1.70). Standard conformal prediction covered 0.51 and 0.37 of oligodendrogliomas, probability sets fell below the target for two subtypes in UTSW-Glioma, and abstention matched on single-subtype calls needed larger sets (1.79 and 2.17). Single-subtype sets, given to 61.8% and 41.7% of patients, were correct in 98.5% and 97.4% when they named glioblastoma but about half the time otherwise. Development-cohort cutoffs fell below the target for glioblastoma (0.84 and 0.79). Class-conditional conformal prediction allowed the model to suggest multiple glioma subtypes when uncertain, reducing the risk of excluding the correct diagnosis, particularly oligodendroglioma. With calibration using comparable patient populations, the correct subtype was included at the intended rate. Single-subtype predictions were most reliable for glioblastoma.

title: The Ataxias as an Example of Rare Diseases: Diagnosis, Genetics, and Treatment.
abstract: Background Ataxias are a group of rare diseases. In the European Union, a disease is defined as rare if its prevalence is less than 5 per 10 000 people. Ataxias are rarer than this threshold, although reliable prevalence estimates are largely lacking. The worldwide mean prevalence of autosomal dominant hereditary ataxias is approximately 2.7 per 100 000 people (95% confidence interval [1.5; 4.0/100 000]), and that of autosomal-recessive ataxias is approximately 3.3 per 100 000 people [1.8; 4.9/100 000]. Ataxias include hereditary (genetic), sporadic degenerative, and acquired types. Methods This narrative review is based on the guidelines of the German Society for Neurology ( Deutsche Gesellschaft für Neurologie ) and on other current reviews, supplemented by the findings of targeted PubMed searches. Results In the more common types of hereditary ataxia, a presumptive diagnosis (spot diagnosis) can already be made on the basis of the history, neurological examination, and brain MRI findings and can then be confirmed by genetic testing. These include Friedreich ataxia, the RFC1-CANVAS syndrome (cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, and vestibular areflexia), and spinocerebellar ataxia types 3 and 27B (SCA3 and SCA27B). When a spot diagnosis is not possible, the diagnosis can often be established by genetic testing (preferably genome-based). Multisystem atrophy of the cerebellar type (MSA-C) arises sporadically. Ataxia with a subacute course suggests an acquired type of ataxia-in particular, immune-mediated ataxias and vitamin B1 deficiency (Wernicke) encephalopathy. Omaveloxolone has been approved for the treatment of Friedreich ataxia. In a phase 2 trial with 103 patients, the clinical severity score (mFARS value, maximum 99 points) improved by a mean of 1.55 points after 48 weeks of treatment, compared with worsening by 0.85 points with placebo. Fampridine is used off-label to treat episodic ataxias, downbeat nystagmus, and SCA27B. Randomized trials have documented the benefit of physiotherapy and regular exercise training for patients with ataxia. Conclusion An increasing number of ataxias can be diagnosed with the improved genetic and immunological diagnostic techniques that are now available. Opportunities for treatment remain limited, but many new therapies are under development, including gene therapy.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Anti-Müllerian Hormone for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background The 2023 international evidence-based guideline for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) conditionally recommended serum anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) as an alternative to ultrasound for diagnosing polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) in adults, marking a significant shift in diagnostic practice. However, the diagnostic accuracy of AMH remains debated, particularly regarding its utility as a standalone test, its application across diverse populations, and its use in adolescents. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Major electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, were searched for diagnostic accuracy studies published until November 2024, and studies evaluating serum AMH against the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS or ultrasound-defined PCOM were included. A bivariate random-effects model was used to pool sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for three key questions: AMH for 1) PCOS diagnosis in adults, 2) PCOM diagnosis in adults, and 3) PCOS diagnosis in adolescents. The Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 tool was used to assess the risk of bias. Results For adult PCOS diagnosis, 83 studies (n = 33,376) were included, yielding a pooled sensitivity of 0.81 (95% CI, 0.78-0.83) and a specificity of 0.89 (95% CI, 0.86-0.91). For adult PCOM diagnosis, six studies (n = 11,436) provided a pooled sensitivity of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.70-0.86) and a specificity of 0.88 (95% CI, 0.77-0.94). In contrast, the analysis for adolescent PCOS (11 studies, n = 1,090) revealed a significantly lower accuracy, with a pooled sensitivity of 0.66 (95% CI, 0.58-0.73) and a specificity of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.71-0.83). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across all analyses. Conclusion The current, updated meta-analysis confirms that serum AMH is a highly specific and moderately sensitive biomarker for diagnosing PCOM and PCOS in adults, supporting its role as an adjunctive diagnostic tool. However, its utility as a standalone test is limited by significant heterogeneity; in addition, its diagnostic performance is further limited in adolescents, providing evidence against its use in such population. Future efforts must focus on the international standardization of AMH assays and the development of population-specific reference values to enhance its clinical utility.

title: Association of CT-Based Sarcopenia, Clinical Frailty, and Nutritional Status With Mortality After Aortic Valve Replacement for Severe Aortic Stenosis.
abstract: Objective This study investigated the association between multiple frailty-related markers-Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) score, and computed tomography (CT)-based sarcopenia-and overall survival after aortic valve replacement (AVR) for severe aortic stenosis (AS), with particular emphasis on the first year after AVR. Materials and methods A total of 407 patients with severe AS who underwent surgical or transcatheter AVR at a tertiary center between November 2020 and December 2022 were retrospectively included. Three frailty-related markers were analyzed: CFS score for functional frailty, CONUT score for nutritional status, and CT-defined sarcopenia for structural muscle depletion. The CONUT score was calculated using serum markers, and sarcopenia was defined according to cohort-specific tertiles of the paravertebral muscle index quantified at the 12th thoracic vertebra (T12) vertebral level using CT. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards analysis was performed to assess the prognostic associations of the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) score and the three frailty-related markers with all-cause mortality after AVR. Results Within 1 year after AVR, 32 patients (7.9%) died. In the overall multivariable analysis, higher CFS scores and CT-defined sarcopenia were independently associated with mortality, with hazard ratios (HRs) of 1.82 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.40-2.38; P < 0.001) and 2.63 (95% CI, 1.22-5.67; P = 0.014), respectively. The STS score and CONUT scores were not associated with survival, with HRs of 1.00 (95% CI, 0.95-1.06; P = 0.883) and 1.05 (95% CI, 0.90-1.22; P = 0.563), respectively. A significant interaction was observed between the CONUT score and sarcopenia. Conclusion Among patients with severe AS undergoing AVR, higher CFS scores and CT-based sarcopenia were independently associated with survival after adjustment for the STS score. The prognostic association of the CONUT score differed according to sarcopenia status. These findings support the incorporation of functional and structural vulnerabilities into risk assessment for patients undergoing AVR for AS; however, the role of nutritional status requires further investigation.

title: Multi-color space image enhancement with weighted fusion and lightweight deep learning framework for AI-based breast cancer histopathology image classification.
abstract: Introduction Variations in Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining, illumination, tissue preparation, and image acquisition affect breast histopathology image analysis, altering nuclear contrast, color consistency, and downstream feature extraction. Separately, prior BreakHis studies have often used image-wise splitting, which can place a patient's images in both training and test sets and inflate performance estimates. Methods To address these two issues, this study introduced a Multi-color Space Image Enhancement (MSIE) approach and evaluates it under strict, leakage-controlled, patient-wise five-fold cross-validation on the BreakHis dataset. MSIE combines H&E color deconvolution, stain normalization, hematoxylin contrast processing with Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE), Hue-Saturation-Value (HSV) space processing, eosin reconstruction, and H&E-weighted fusion. Before model training, the dataset underwent a decoded-pixel Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) integrity check, and 125 duplicate images were removed, reducing the dataset from 7,909 to 7,784. The Lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (LCNN) model is trained and tested on MSIE and original RGB images using an identical architecture and patient partitions, and MobileNetV2, ResNet50, DenseNet169, and EfficientNetB0 are evaluated under the same protocol to assess efficiency-accuracy trade-offs across model capacities. Results Performance is assessed at the image and patient levels using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 Score, Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC AUC), and Precision-Recall Area Under the Curve (PR AUC), alongside Fusion-coefficient sensitivity, magnification-specific performance, computational efficiency, Grad-CAM visualization, and independent BACH testing. At the patient level, original RGB achieved an accuracy of 0.8397 ± 0.0325 and F1-score of 0.8789 ± 0.0326, versus a mean accuracy of 0.7522 ± 0.2218 and F1-score of 0.7632 ± 0.2734 for MSIE. MSIE, however, produced a slightly higher mean ROC-AUC (0.9024 ± 0.1274 versus 0.8952 ± 0.1023). Higher-capacity ImageNet-pretrained architectures performed better on MSIE inputs, with EfficientNetB0 achieving the highest mean patient-level accuracy (0.9007 ± 0.0718) and ROC-AUC (0.9707 ± 0.0354). Independent evaluation on the BACH dataset using frozen BreaKHis-trained MSIE-LCNN models yielded an accuracy of 0.7056 and an ROC-AUC of 0.7012, indicating substantial cross-dataset domain shift. Discussion Overall, MSIE provides a stain-aware representation whose downstream benefits are not universal and depend on the classifier architecture, fusion balance, operating point, and dataset domain, thereby supporting leakage-controlled and externally validated assessment of histopathology processing methods rather than claims of immediate clinical translation.

Introduction

Variations in Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining, illumination, tissue preparation, and image acquisition affect breast histopathology image analysis, altering nuclear contrast, color consistency, and downstream feature extraction. Separately, prior BreakHis studies have often used image-wise splitting, which can place a patient's images in both training and test sets and inflate performance estimates.

Methods

To address these two issues, this study introduced a Multi-color Space Image Enhancement (MSIE) approach and evaluates it under strict, leakage-controlled, patient-wise five-fold cross-validation on the BreakHis dataset. MSIE combines H&E color deconvolution, stain normalization, hematoxylin contrast processing with Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE), Hue-Saturation-Value (HSV) space processing, eosin reconstruction, and H&E-weighted fusion. Before model training, the dataset underwent a decoded-pixel Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) integrity check, and 125 duplicate images were removed, reducing the dataset from 7,909 to 7,784. The Lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (LCNN) model is trained and tested on MSIE and original RGB images using an identical architecture and patient partitions, and MobileNetV2, ResNet50, DenseNet169, and EfficientNetB0 are evaluated under the same protocol to assess efficiency-accuracy trade-offs across model capacities.

Results

Performance is assessed at the image and patient levels using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 Score, Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC AUC), and Precision-Recall Area Under the Curve (PR AUC), alongside Fusion-coefficient sensitivity, magnification-specific performance, computational efficiency, Grad-CAM visualization, and independent BACH testing. At the patient level, original RGB achieved an accuracy of 0.8397 ± 0.0325 and F1-score of 0.8789 ± 0.0326, versus a mean accuracy of 0.7522 ± 0.2218 and F1-score of 0.7632 ± 0.2734 for MSIE. MSIE, however, produced a slightly higher mean ROC-AUC (0.9024 ± 0.1274 versus 0.8952 ± 0.1023). Higher-capacity ImageNet-pretrained architectures performed better on MSIE inputs, with EfficientNetB0 achieving the highest mean patient-level accuracy (0.9007 ± 0.0718) and ROC-AUC (0.9707 ± 0.0354). Independent evaluation on the BACH dataset using frozen BreaKHis-trained MSIE-LCNN models yielded an accuracy of 0.7056 and an ROC-AUC of 0.7012, indicating substantial cross-dataset domain shift.

Discussion

Overall, MSIE provides a stain-aware representation whose downstream benefits are not universal and depend on the classifier architecture, fusion balance, operating point, and dataset domain, thereby supporting leakage-controlled and externally validated assessment of histopathology processing methods rather than claims of immediate clinical translation.

title: Biomechanical effects of different suture pretension levels in suture-bridge repair of supraspinatus tendon tears: a finite element analysis.
abstract: Objective The optimal initial suture pretension during suture-bridge repair of full-thickness supraspinatus tendon tears remains uncertain and is largely determined by the surgeon's experience. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different suture pretensions on the mechanical environment of the tendon-bone interface and to provide a biomechanical reference for intraoperative tension control. Methods A three-dimensional finite element model of the shoulder joint was reconstructed from computed tomography data of a healthy adult volunteer. A full-thickness supraspinatus tear was simulated and repaired using a double-row suture-bridge configuration. Seven total pretension levels (30-90 N, in 10 N increments) and three shoulder abduction positions (10°, 20°, and 30°) were combined to generate 21 loading conditions. The mean contact pressure, effective contact area, relative interfacial displacement, and tendon-side von Mises stress were analyzed. Results Increasing pretension increased the mean tendon-bone contact pressure at all abduction angles. At 20° of abduction, the mean contact pressure increased from 0.382 MPa to 0.856 MPa. The peak tendon-side von Mises stress also increased with pretension, reaching a maximum of 4.533 MPa in the 30°/90 N condition. The effective contact area changed only slightly at 10° of abduction, decreased from 181.4 mm 2 to 169.5 mm 2 at 20°, and reached relatively high values at 50-60 N at 30°. High-stress regions were mainly concentrated around the medial-row suture perforation sites and expanded as pretension increased. Conclusion Suture pretension improved tendon-bone compression and initial interfacial stability, but higher pretension increased local pressure and tendon stress concentration. Within the tested configurations, 50-60 N represented an intermediate, condition-dependent range rather than a universal clinical target.

title: Ultrasound-responsive microbubble platforms in lung cancer: mechanisms, molecular targeting, and therapeutic applications.
abstract: Lung cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, while the heterogeneous tumor microenvironment, abnormal vasculature, elevated interstitial fluid pressure, hypoxia, and dense extracellular matrix substantially limit the efficacy of conventional systemic therapies. Ultrasound-responsive microbubbles (MBs) have emerged as versatile theranostic platforms capable of overcoming several of these delivery barriers through externally controlled acoustic cavitation. This review comprehensively discusses the evolution, physicochemical characteristics, composition, and functional mechanisms of MB-based systems for lung cancer diagnosis and therapy. Particular emphasis is placed on stable and inertial cavitation, sonoporation, microstreaming, vascular permeabilization, and enhanced transport of therapeutic agents into tumor tissue. The diagnostic potential of targeted MBs for contrast-enhanced ultrasound, molecular imaging, perfusion assessment, and super-resolution visualization of tumor vasculature is highlighted. Therapeutic applications encompassing chemotherapeutics, nucleic acids, microRNAs, oxygen delivery, immunotherapy, and combination strategies with radiotherapy are critically examined. The review also discusses molecularly targeted MBs, nanoparticle-MB hybrids, and ultrasound-triggered modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment. Despite promising preclinical outcomes, challenges involving pulmonary acoustic attenuation, short circulation time, biodistribution, treatment parameter standardization, manufacturing, safety, and regulatory requirements remain. Emerging theranostic, hybrid, and artificial intelligence-assisted platforms may facilitate personalized and clinically translatable microbubble-based precision therapy for lung cancer.

title: Prognostic value of model for end-stage liver disease excluding international normalized ratio score combined with late gadolinium enhancement in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
abstract: Introduction Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is one of the main subtypes of heart failure (HF). Model for end-stage liver disease excluding international normalized ratio (MELD-XI) score and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) each independently predict adverse prognosis in HF patients. Methods This retrospective study enrolled adult HFrEF patients admitted to Qilu Hospital of Shandong University between September 2018 and January 2023. The primary endpoint was defined as a composite endpoint of rehospitalization for HF and all-cause mortality. Multivariate Cox regression model was established to evaluate the effects of LGE and MELD-XI score on the primary endpoint. We also evaluate the incremental prognostic value of adding the MELD-XI score to the model. Results A total of 246 HFrEF patients were included and 55 patients reached the primary endpoint during follow-up. In the adjusted Cox regression model, for each standard deviation increase in LGE and MELD-XI score, the hazard ratios (HRs) for primary endpoint were 1.52 (95% CI: 1.23-1.88) and 1.60 (95% CI: 1.31-1.94), respectively. Adding MELD-XI score into model improved its incremental prognostic performance [ Δ C-Statistic: 0.052 (95% CI: 0.001-0.092), p = 0.039; Continuous NRI: 0.399 (95% CI: 0.077-0.532), p = 0.027; IDI: 0.094 (95% CI: 0.018-0.174), p = 0.010]. Conclusions Both CMR-assessed LGE and MELD-XI score were associated with adverse outcomes in patients with HFrEF. Combining these two indicators provided complementary prognostic information for HFrEF patients.

title: Discordant low-gradient aortic stenosis: a phenotype-first, likelihood-tiered multimodality imaging framework.
abstract: Discordant low-gradient aortic stenosis (AS), commonly defined by the aortic valve area (AVA) ≤1.0 cm 2 with mean gradient <40 mmHg and peak velocity <4.0 m/s, is reported in up to 40% of patients evaluated for AS in selected cohorts. Current guidelines and consensus documents outline echocardiographic quality control, haemodynamic phenotype assignment, dobutamine stress echocardiography (DSE), CT aortic valve calcium scoring (CT-AVC), and integrated assessment, yet uncertainty persists when haemodynamic, structural, symptomatic, and myocardial findings diverge. This narrative review proposes a phenotype-first, likelihood-tiered multimodality framework that adds four operational elements to current guidance: routine documentation of transvalvular flow rate, phenotype-specific interpretation of DSE and CT-AVC, separation of valve severity adjudication from myocardial risk refinement, and structured reporting of residual uncertainty. DSE with projected AVA is favoured for flow-dependent severity assessment in classical low-flow low-gradient AS, whereas CT-AVC likelihood categories are emphasised in preserved-ejection-fraction low-gradient phenotypes and after inconclusive DSE. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance, global longitudinal strain, extracellular volume fraction, and cardiac damage staging are used as prognostic and counselling adjuncts, not stand-alone triggers for valve intervention. Indeterminate cases are reported as unresolved discordance with the basis of uncertainty stated explicitly. The approach is intended to improve Heart Team communication and requires prospective validation before use as a treatment algorithm.

title: Cardiac CT in ANOCA, INOCA, and MINOCA: a structured narrative review of evidence, applications, and limitations.
abstract: Cardiac computed tomography (CT) depicts coronary anatomy and provides additional physiological and myocardial measurements in angina or ischemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries (ANOCA/INOCA) and acute non-obstructive presentations. This structured narrative review examines what these measurements establish about anatomy, vasomotor mechanisms, prognosis, and clinical utility. Six-domain searches of PubMed, Embase, and CENTRAL, supplemented by citation-based sources and ClinicalTrials.gov, were updated through 23 September 2026. The bibliographic inventory contains 154 publications; selection was targeted, involving single-assessor historical screening and revision-stage triage rather than a systematic-review process. Contemporary MINOCA denotes myocardial injury with non-obstructive coronary arteries as a working diagnosis; historical study definitions are preserved. Conventional coronary CT angiography depicts plaque, anomalies, myocardial bridging, and selected coronary-wall abnormalities. Plaque and pericoronary-fat associations vary with the population and reference standard. Small syndrome-specific studies and related cohorts provide limited diagnostic evidence; prognostic associations do not validate vasomotor endotyping. CT-derived fractional flow reserve concerns epicardial pressure loss, while CT perfusion does not independently identify a vasomotor mechanism. Late iodine enhancement and CT-derived extracellular volume provide myocardial information, but agreement with individual cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) measurements does not establish equivalence to multiparametric CMR. After non-obstructive invasive angiography, additional CT should answer a defined residual question and justify contrast exposure, radiation, and diagnostic delay. The evidence examined in this review does not establish that an advanced CT biomarker strategy improves mechanism-specific treatment selection or patient outcomes in ANOCA/INOCA or an acute MINOCA pathway.

title: Patient-level diagnostic performance of myocardial contrast echocardiography using ultrasound-enhancing agents after acute myocardial infarction: comparison with radionuclide perfusion-metabolism imaging.
abstract: Objective This study evaluated the patient-level diagnostic performance and agreement of myocardial contrast echocardiography (MCE) for assessing myocardial viability after acute myocardial infarction (AMI), using combined radionuclide perfusion-metabolism imaging as the reference standard. Methods This retrospective diagnostic-comparison study included 141 patients with AMI who underwent MCE and reference radionuclide perfusion-metabolism imaging between February 2017 and February 2023. Imaging was generally performed during the subacute phase, 7-14 days after symptom onset. Reference assessment combined 99 mTc-MIBI myocardial perfusion imaging with 18 F-FDG metabolic imaging. The standardized 17-segment left ventricular model was used as an anatomical framework for image interpretation; however, because individual segment-level classifications were not systematically archived, diagnostic performance was evaluated at the patient level. MCE examinations were interpreted independently by experienced cardiologists blinded to the reference imaging results, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and Cohen's kappa were calculated with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Reference imaging classified 91 patients as having viable myocardium and 50 as having non-viable myocardium. MCE yielded 79 true-positive, 44 true-negative, 6 false-positive, and 12 false-negative classifications. Patient-level sensitivity was 86.81% (95% CI, 78.35%-92.29%), specificity was 88.00% (95% CI, 76.20%-94.38%), and overall accuracy was 87.23% (95% CI, 80.72%-91.77%). PPV was 92.94% (95% CI, 85.44%-96.72%), and NPV was 78.57% (95% CI, 66.18%-87.29%). Agreement between MCE and reference imaging was substantial (Cohen's κ = 0.728; 95% CI, 0.612-0.845; P < 0.001). Conclusion MCE demonstrated substantial patient-level agreement with radionuclide perfusion-metabolism imaging for post-AMI myocardial viability assessment. These findings support its potential role as a complementary diagnostic imaging modality under the evaluated conditions. However, the present study did not assess subsequent functional recovery, ventricular remodeling, revascularization benefit, treatment decisions, or clinical outcomes; therefore, no conclusions regarding patient-management benefit or prognostic utility can be drawn from these data.

title: SynForge-Cardio: a unified multimodal synthetic dataset generation framework for privacy-preserving cardiovascular AI.
abstract: Multimodal cardiovascular AI systems benefit from jointly available chest radiographs, 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs), and structured electronic health record (EHR) variables. In practice, multi-institutional model development is constrained by privacy regulations, institutional data silos, and class imbalance for less common findings. Existing open-source synthetic data tools are largely modality-specific: tabular libraries such as Synthetic Data Vault (SDV)/Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN), image generators based on latent diffusion, and time-series methods such as Time-series Generative Adversarial Network (TimeGAN) each require its own setup, configuration, and validation. This study presents SynForge-Cardio, a multimodality orchestration framework for prompt-driven synthetic dataset generation across chest X-ray (CXR), 12-lead ECG, and EHR modalities. Rather than introducing a new generative backbone, SynForge-Cardio coordinates established components-latent diffusion with optional low-rank adaptation for CXR; parametric and bounded morphology-preserving augmentation (with an optional TimeGAN path) for ECG; and size-aware routing among jitter augmentation, Gaussian copula, and CTGAN/Tabular Variational Autoencoder for EHR-behind a shared clinical prompt interface, a rule-based router, and a postgeneration quality/privacy reporting layer. The three modalities were generated independently from separate datasets; the framework does not perform patient-level joint synthesis and makes no claim of anatomical or physiological consistency across modalities. This system is implemented as a FastAPI backend with a React frontend and can run on a single workstation GPU. Herein, we formalize the orchestration objective, specify modality-wise models and metrics [Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), dynamic time warping (DTW), power spectral density similarity, Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics, correlation preservation, and distance-to-closest-record privacy screening], and describe an evaluation protocol on public corpora (NIH Chest X-ray14, PTB-XL, and the UCI Cleveland Heart Disease dataset), including a four-regime train-on-synthetic/test-on-real (TSTR) utility analysis with five random seeds. On the framework alone, we measured 94.6% modality-routing accuracy, 100% direct-vs.-routed generation equivalence on the evaluated cases, 59 unnecessary generator calls avoided, and 100% validation/reporting completeness (1,105/1,108 tests pass, 3 skipped). Downstream-utility results were mixed: augmenting a 25%-real training set with synthetic data changed the held-out AUROC by -0.041 to +0.050 across three CXR tasks (none significant at five seeds); by +0.019 for ECG MI-vs.-NORM [produced by mode B (bounded real-waveform augmentation, whose synthetic samples can be matched to their true source recording at top-1 ≈ 42.7-43.4%, and hence, mode B is not an independently learned generative model)]; and by +0.017 for EHR heart disease classification, which is not evidence of benefit given the 61-record hold-out set (the test-set bootstrap 95% CI for the difference includes zero). Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV acquisition was not completed because credentialed access was unavailable; all reported EHR results were UCI-based. SynForge-Cardio is intended as a practical, reproducible research framework for privacy-conscious cardiovascular data augmentation and prototype development.

title: Case Report: Balancing atypical femoral fracture healing and bone metastasis control.
abstract: Background Bone-modifying agents (BMAs) represent standard supportive therapy for patients with bone metastases to mitigate skeletal-related events (SREs). Alongside improved cancer survival, cumulative antiresorptive exposure renders atypical femoral fracture (AFF) an important yet infrequent complication. For patients with active metastatic disease, clinical management poses unique challenges, since discontinuation of antiresorptive agents may elevate skeletal-related risk while sustained suppression may impede fracture healing. Case presentation A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman with metastatic breast cancer had received zoledronic acid (4 mg intravenously every 3 months) for 4 years. Because of progression of bone metastases and chest/back pain, treatment was changed to denosumab (120 mg monthly). After three doses, she developed bilateral thigh pain after a minor torsion injury, and radiographs demonstrated bilateral transverse femoral shaft fractures with lateral cortical thickening. Bilateral antegrade intramedullary nailing was performed. Intraoperative bone marrow pathology showed no tumor infiltration. Denosumab was discontinued. Two months later, because of persistent severe osteoporosis and increased bone resorption (β-CTX 0.65 ng/mL), zoledronic acid 4 mg every 12 weeks was restarted. Outcome Eight months after fixation, both fractures achieved radiographic healing with callus formation; no new skeletal-related events were documented during follow-up. Serum β-CTX decreased to 0.35 ng/mL. This clinical course suggests that de-escalated zoledronic acid therapy was temporally associated with fracture healing while sustaining continuous antiresorptive effects in this individual patient. Conclusion This case underscores the diagnostic necessity of distinguishing AFF from metastatic pathological fracture, as well as the therapeutic trade-off between fracture healing and sustained skeletal protection. Sequential antiresorptive exposure, notably prolonged bisphosphonate administration followed by denosumab, warrants vigilant clinical screening for potential AFF. Post-denosumab therapeutic strategies should take rebound bone turnover into consideration. The proposed risk-stratified surveillance framework is evidence-informed but remains unvalidated and should not be interpreted as formal clinical guidance.

title: Application of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid cancer.
abstract: Thyroid cancer is one of the most common endocrine malignancies, and its rising incidence has increased the demand for more accurate and efficient diagnostic and management strategies. Current clinical management mainly relies on ultrasonography, fine-needle aspiration (FNA), surgery, radioactive iodine therapy, thyroid-stimulating hormone suppression, and systemic treatment in selected advanced cases. However, substantial interobserver variability, indeterminate cytology, and heterogeneity in tumor behavior still complicate diagnosis and risk stratification. In thyroid cancer, AI(Artificial intelligence) -assisted models have been applied to ultrasound, CT, MRI, cytology, histopathology, and genomic data, with promising performance in distinguishing benign from malignant nodules, predicting lymph node metastasis and key mutations, and supporting individualized management. This review critically synthesizes evidence across these applications, focusing on study design, validation strategies, generalizability, and clinical relevance. It also examines explainable AI, emerging foundation models, and regulatory and implementation challenges. Although many models report high diagnostic or predictive performance, these results alone do not establish improvements in clinical decision-making or patient outcomes. Prospective clinical validation, cost-effectiveness assessment, and evaluation of integration into clinical workflows are needed to determine whether AI provides meaningful benefits over standard care.

title: Opportunistic application of machine learning for bone health stratification in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
abstract: Purpose The primary objective of this study was to compare the performance of various machine learning (ML) models in the opportunistic screening of abnormal bone mineral density (BMD) among type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) patients using routine non-contrast-enhanced chest CT. Materials and methods A total of 249 T2DM patients (age range, 40-97 years; mean ± standard deviation, 60.93 ± 11.49 years) who underwent chest CT with quantitative CT (QCT) analysis were retrospectively enrolled between January 2021 and June 2024. Patients were randomly split at a 7:3 ratio into a training set (n=175) and an internal test set (n=74). Semi-automatic segmentation of the L1 vertebral body was performed using 3D Slicer, and 2273 radiomic features were extracted via the Research Portal V1.1 workstation. Six radiomics-based ML models were constructed; their predictive performance and stability for distinguishing normal versus abnormal BMD were evaluated and compared. Results Among the T2DM patients included, the incidence of abnormal BMD was 40.56% (101/249). Fifteen radiomic features were selected using the minimum redundancy-maximum relevance (MRMR) algorithm and incorporated into six ML models (RF, SVMRadial, SVMLinear, NNet, xgbLinear and KNNs). In nested cross-validation, the SVMLinear model achieved the better predictive performance (accuracy: 0.906 ± 0.032; area under the curve [AUC]: 0.945 ± 0.028), followed by the NNet model (accuracy: 0.906 ± 0.031; AUC: 0.941 ± 0.029). In terms of stability, the SVMLinear model exhibited greater robustness against data perturbation (relative standard deviation [RSD] of mean accuracy: 3.54%; RSD of mean AUC: 3.04%). Conclusions The ML models enable opportunistic prediction of BMD status from chest CT in patients with T2DM. Specifically, the L1-vertebra radiomics-based SVMLinear model achieves a favorable balance of discrimination ability and stability, and may serve as a useful tool for opportunistic clinical screening for abnormal BMD in this patient population.

title: The full spectrum of thyroid late effects following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in pediatrics: insights from a large multicenter cohort.
abstract: Introduction Thyroid disorders are among the most prevalent late sequelae of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). While total body irradiation (TBI) is an established risk factor, the toxicity of alkylating agent-based conditioning regimens remains poorly characterized. The present study aimed to: i) quantify the cumulative incidence (CI) of thyroid late effects in a large multicenter pediatric cohort; ii) identify the independent risk determinants of HSCT-related thyroid disorders; iii) assess the specific detrimental role of chemo-only conditioning regimens; iv) characterize longitudinal thyroid volumetric trajectories following HSCT. Methods Multicenter retrospective observational study enrolling 637 pediatric HSCT survivors transplanted between 1999 and 2023 across three referral Centers. Conditioning regimens included: TBI (40%), busulfan (32%), treosulfan (18%), other (10%). Endocrine surveillance encompassed 6-12-monthly thyroid function tests and ultrasound assessment over a mean follow-up of 11.0 ± 6.4 years. Results The 20-year CI achieved 43.1% for thyroid function disorders (TFD) and 71.2% for nodules. Concerning the conditioning regimen, the 20-year CI of TFD was 54%, 35% and 21% for TBI, busulfan and treosulfan, respectively (p=0.026). The CI of TFD was statistically lower following treosulfan than busulfan (p=0.039). Compared to treosulfan, both TBI (HR 2.39, p=0.006) and busulfan (HR 1.77, p=0.08) conferred an increased risk of TFD on multivariate analysis. Concerning ultrasonographic findings, the 18-year CI of thyroid nodules following TBI overtly exceeded chemo-only regimens, while treosulfan and busulfan showed comparable longitudinal trendlines (p 0.82). The right lobe anteroposterior diameter (RLD) Z-score was used as an indirect indicator of thyroid volume. Longitudinal ultrasonographic assessment revealed significantly greater RLD Z-scores following treosulfan compared with busulfan (p=0.002) and TBI (p<0.001). Finally, age<10 years at HSCT (p=0.013), severe graft versus host disease (p=0.036), TBI (P = 0.05) and elevated BMI (p=0.04) were independent determinants of the need for hormonal replacement therapy. Conclusions Treosulfan-based conditioning is associated with the lowest cumulative functional thyroid morbidity and the most favorable longitudinal volumetric profile among myeloablative regimens, outperforming busulfan on both endpoints and a lesser degree of thyrocyte damage.

title: Integrated imaging, body composition, and systemic immune-inflammatory profiling for non-invasive prediction of HER2 status in endometrial cancer.
abstract: Objectives Preoperative evaluation of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status in endometrial cancer (EC) is clinically important for molecular stratification and treatment planning. This study aimed to develop a non-invasive predictive model integrating functional MRI-derived tumor characteristics, CT-derived body composition, and systemic immune-inflammatory markers for identifying HER2-positive EC. Methods In this single-center retrospective study, 75 patients with pathologically confirmed EC (41 HER2-positive, 34 HER2-negative) who underwent preoperative 3.0 T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including amide proton transfer-weighted (APTw) imaging and intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) diffusion-weighted imaging, and chest CT between August 2019 and June 2026 were evaluated. Quantitative MRI parameters, including APT values, the slow apparent diffusion coefficient (D), fast apparent diffusion coefficient (D*), and perfusion fraction (f), and CT-derived body composition, including visceral adipose tissue (VAT), subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), skeletal muscle (SM) and intramuscular adipose tissue (IMAT), were extracted. Systemic immune-inflammatory parameters including neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR), monocyte to lymphocyte ratio (MLR), platelet to lymphocyte ratio (PLR) and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) were calculated. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent risk factors and build predictive models, with diagnostic efficacy assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis and internal validation using 1000-resample bootstrap. Results The HER2 (+) group demonstrated significantly higher APT values (2.76% vs. 2.44%), D* values (3.23 × 10- 3 mm 2 /s vs. 1.88 × 10- 3 mm 2 /s), f values (0.22 vs. 0.19), SAT area (138.38 cm 2 vs. 112.73 cm 2 ), and MLR values (0.19 vs. 0.14) compared with the HER2 (-) group, whereas lower D values (0.59 × 10- 3 mm 2 /s vs. 0.67 × 10- 3 mm 2 /s) were observed in the HER2 (+) group. Multivariable logistic regression analysis identified APT (OR = 9.368, P = 0.011), f (OR = 8.303, P = 0.002), SAT (OR = 1.017, P = 0.033), and MLR (OR = 8.336, P = 0.006) as independent predictors of HER2 positivity. The integrated model incorporating APT value, f, SAT, and MLR achieved an AUC of 0.879, sensitivity of 87.8%, and specificity of 79.4%. Conclusion An integrated model combining tumor imaging characteristics, body composition parameters, and systemic immune-inflammatory markers may provide a non-invasive approach for preoperative prediction of HER2-positive EC.

title: Pituitary residual tumor detection: incremental value of multimodal assessment.
abstract: Introduction Postoperative residual tumor is associated with regrowth and recurrence in pituitary adenomas, making maximal safe resection an important therapeutic goal. We evaluated the incremental contribution of microscopy, endoscopic inspection, and 3.0-T intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging (iMRI) to residual tumor detection and assessment of the planned extent of resection. Methods In this retrospective single-center cohort study, 120 consecutive eligible patients undergoing transsphenoidal surgery for pituitary adenoma underwent sequential microsurgical resection, endoscopic inspection, and iMRI. Results Initial endoscopic inspection confirmed the planned extent of resection in 95/120 patients (79.2%) and indicated further resection in 25/120 (20.8%). After any indicated further resection, repeat endoscopic inspection confirmed planned extent of resection achievement before iMRI in all 120 patients. title: Radiomics- based biomarkers for immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer: advances, challenges, and future perspectives in biological interpretation and clinical translation.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have improved outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet treatment benefit remains heterogeneous and resistance is common. Genomic alterations, tumor microenvironment (TME) remodeling, and metabolic reprogramming across spatial and temporal scales that are incompletely captured by single-site tissue sampling. Radiomics extracts quantitative features from routine images and offers a framework for investigating macroscopic correlates of these processes. This narrative review critically examines computed tomography (CT) and fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/CT (¹ 8 F-FDG PET/CT) radiomics in relation to oncogenic alterations, immune and stromal phenotypes, programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, tumor mutational burden, and metabolic-immune interactions in NSCLC. It should be highlighted that such observed statistical links only generate plausible biological hypotheses and do not constitute experimental proof of true mechanistic relationships. Rather than merely summarizing predictive model performance, we emphasize evidence boundaries and interpretive caveats for radiomic-TME associations. We further elaborate on key translational bottlenecks including limited reproducibility, technical standardization deficits, and retrospective-model overfitting. We discuss ongoing efforts toward cross-scale multi-omics integration, alongside the promises and inherent limitations of explainable artificial intelligence and federated learning for clinical translation. To move beyond purely predictive tools toward mechanism-aware decision-support systems, future radiomic research requires prospective multicenter validation, rigorous data harmonization, and combined analyses integrating spatial transcriptomics, digital pathology, and circulating biomarkers for precision immuno-oncology.

title: Neoadjuvant treatment is associated with fibrotic and transcriptional remodeling of tumor-draining lymph nodes in rectal cancer.
abstract: Background Neoadjuvant treatment is associated with reduced lymph-node yield in rectal cancer, but the accompanying changes in tumor-draining lymph nodes (TDLNs) remain incompletely characterized. Methods We analyzed Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results data, a 178-patient institutional cohort, quantitative histopathology of 447 histologically negative TDLNs from 159 patients, and bulk RNA sequencing of 30 nodes from 24 patients. Institutional comparisons distinguished a radiotherapy-containing treatment pathway (RT) from management without preoperative radiotherapy (NRT); in the institutional clinical cohort, all 105 RT patients and 10 of 73 NRT patients received neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Pathology models accounted for patient clustering, and RNA counts were aggregated within patients. Results Recorded preoperative radiotherapy was associated with lower examined-node counts in Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER). In the institutional cohort, the expanded pretreatment-adjusted incidence-rate ratio was 0.83 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.67-1.02]; pretreatment-covariate overlap weighting yielded 0.80 (95% CI, 0.66-0.96). RT-group nodes were more fibrotic and smaller, with lower germinal-center and lymphoid-tissue area fractions. Patient-level RNA-seq identified 4,446 differentially expressed genes, with higher extracellular-matrix and angiogenic programs and lower antigen-receptor and B-cell-receptor signaling. Selected pathway directions were retained across sensitivity analyses. Computational deconvolution provided supportive estimates of relative cell composition. Conclusion A radiotherapy-containing neoadjuvant treatment pathway, including chemoradiotherapy in the institutional clinical, pathology, and RNA-seq cohorts, was associated with lower node yield and structural and transcriptional differences in TDLNs. These findings characterize the nodal structural and transcriptional phenotype associated with neoadjuvant treatment.

title: Combined CD8 and granzyme B PET/CT reveals divergent immune responses to radiotherapy plus PD-1 blockade.
abstract: Background Combined radiotherapy (RT) and PD-1 blockade can elicit durable antitumor immunity, yet responses remain heterogeneous and difficult to predict with conventional anatomical imaging. Noninvasive visualization of functional immune activity could provide mechanistic insights into treatment response. Here, we evaluated a dual-tracer PET imaging strategy targeting CD8 + T-cell localization and granzyme B (GZMB)-associated cytotoxic activity during radiotherapy plus PD-1 blockade. Methods Female BALB/c mice bearing CT26 colorectal or 4T1 breast tumors were divided into phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), PD-1 blockade, radiotherapy (RT), or combined PD-1 blockade plus RT groups. 89 Zr-DFO-anti-CD8 PET/CT characterized baseline immune phenotype and treatment-associated CD8+ cell localization, whereas serial 68 Ga-NOTA-granzyme B-targeted probe (GZP) PET/CT assessed early granzyme B-associated effector activity. Tumor uptake was quantified as percentage injected dose per cubic centimeter (%ID/cc), and imaging findings were related to tumor growth and immunohistochemical staining. Results In CT26 tumors, the combination group showed significantly increased 89 Zr-DFO-anti-CD8 uptake at 120 hours (10.09 ± 1.05%ID/cc versus 7.01 ± 0.60%ID/cc in PBS; p < 0.001) and increased 68 Ga-NOTA-GZP uptake on day 9 (0.64 ± 0.13%ID/cc; p < 0.05 versus PBS and RT and p < 0.01 versus PD-1 blockade). In 4T1 tumors, combination treatment showed increased 89 Zr-DFO-anti-CD8 uptake at 72 hours (5.88 ± 0.60%ID/cc; p < 0.05 versus PBS group), whereas mean GZP uptake was not significantly different from monotherapy groups. Importantly, animals classified as responders based on a pre-defined day-20 tumor-growth inhibition (TGI) threshold exhibited higher GZP uptake on days 6 and 9 compared with non-responders. Conclusion Dual-tracer PET provides complementary information on CD8 + T-cell localization and GZMB-associated cytotoxic activity. Notably, the model-dependent CD8 and GZP signals in 4T1 tumors suggest that T-cell recruitment may not necessarily reflect effective cytotoxic function, supporting the complementary value of functional imaging alongside localization-based approaches. The findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating and support further preclinical and prospective clinical investigation.

title: Differential LAG3 expression in intestinal tissue reveals a dual-pathology model of steroid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease.
abstract: Introduction Acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD) of the gastrointestinal tract remains a leading cause of non-relapse mortality following allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation, and steroid-refractory intestinal aGVHD carries a particularly poor prognosis. CD8 + T cells are critical effectors of intestinal tissue injury, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying their pathogenic role remain incompletely understood, especially in the steroid-refractory state. Methods This study aimed to identify key biomarker genes associated with CD8 + T cell-mediated intestinal aGVHD and to characterize their expression dynamics in the steroid-refractory state. Integrative bioinformatics analysis was performed using the Gene Expression Omnibus dataset GSE79083 (a CD8 + T cell-dependent murine aGVHD model), with a human dataset (GSE134662) for independent validation. Hub genes were prioritized through protein-protein interaction network analysis and random forest machine learning. A murine aGVHD model was established for validation via clinical score, qRT-PCR, histopathology, and immunofluorescence double staining. Results Lag3 was identified as the top-ranked gene with high diagnostic discrimination. In the murine model, Lag3 was markedly upregulated in intestinal tissue of the aGVHD group, and immunofluorescence confirmed CD8 + LAG3 + T cell infiltration of the intestinal mucosa. Notably, the steroid-refractory group exhibited more severe colonic histopathological injury. In this group, Lag3 expression was significantly lower than in the aGVHD group despite persistent CD8 + T cell infiltration. A similar expression pattern was observed in the human dataset. Conclusion The reduction of Lag3 despite persistent severe tissue injury suggests that glucocorticoid-resistant CD8 + T cells may have escaped checkpoint-mediated restraint. These findings suggest a dual-pathology framework for steroid-refractory intestinal aGVHD, involving both effector mechanisms independent of LAG3 and impaired epithelial repair. Whether targeting both processes in combination would be beneficial remains to be tested.
