title: Serial Circulating Tumour Cell Monitoring During Androgen Deprivation and Docetaxel Therapies Identifies Poor Prognostic Metastatic Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Background/objectives Adding docetaxel to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) prolongs survival in metastatic prostate cancer, but not all patients benefit, and no early biomarker identifies individuals with resistant disease. We assessed whether serial circulating tumour cell (CTC) sampling adds prognostic information beyond a pre-treatment sample. Methods CTCs were enriched by size and deformability (Parsortix ® ) and phenotyped as epithelial (CK+/VIM-/CD45-), mesenchymal (CK-/VIM+/CD45-), or EMTing (CK+/VIM+/CD45-) at four time points in 61 patients treated with ADT and docetaxel (43 hormone-sensitive; 18 resistant, exploratory). Results With longer follow-up, our previously reported baseline CTC predictors remained associated with overall survival (OS). In hormone-sensitive patients, baseline ≥ 6 total (HR 3.21, p = 0.007) and epithelial CTCs ( p = 0.017) were associated with shorter OS. Across baseline, early, and late treatment, the OS hazard ratio for epithelial CTCs fell (2.59, 2.29, 2.11), yet for ≥3 mesenchymal CTCs rose (1.99, 2.99, 4.08). No single time point result survived false-discovery-rate correction. During early treatment, radiographic responders had fewer mesenchymal CTCs than non-responders (median 0 vs. 2.5, p = 0.032), whereas PSA did not differ ( p = 0.642). Persistence of ≥3 mesenchymal CTCs from baseline to late treatment identified the poorest outcome ( n = 3; median OS 17.3 months vs. not reached) and survived false-discovery-rate correction (q = 0.019). Late treatment mesenchymal CTCs added value to baseline PSA ( p = 0.024) and ALP ( p = 0.019) and added potential value to the best baseline marker (≥6 CTCs, p = 0.125), identifying some high-risk patients with baseline < 6 CTCs. Conclusions Early on-treatment CTC samples may help predict response, while late treatment mesenchymal CTCs may add to baseline clinical markers. These hypothesis-generating findings require validation in a larger prospective cohort.

title: Attention-Based Dual-Branch Deep Learning for Overall Survival Prediction in Patients with Brain Metastases Using MRI: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
abstract: Objectives : To develop and validate an attention-based deep learning (DL) model to predict overall survival (OS) in patients with brain metastases (BM) using pre-treatment magnetic resonance image (MRI). Methods : A total of 216 BM patients treated with radiotherapy or neurosurgical resection were retrospectively enrolled from two hospitals and divided into training ( n = 128), internal validation ( n = 56), and external validation ( n = 32) cohorts. Three feature aggregation methods and seven radiomics models were developed to predict OS. A DL model named DeepBMSurv, incorporating a cross-attention mechanism, was built using pre-treatment MR images. Its prognostic performance was compared with radiomics models and graded prognostic assessment (GPA). A nomogram integrating GPA, radiomics score (Rad-score) and DL score (DL_RiskScore) was also developed. Model performance was assessed by the concordance index (C-index). Results : Among the radiomics models, the RadScore mean model showed the most stable discrimination across cohorts, with C-index values of 0.685, 0.672, and 0.671 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts. DeepBMSurv achieved numerically higher C-indices than both the radiomics model and GPA model, with C-indices of 0.806 vs. 0.685 vs. 0.620 in the training cohort, 0.755 vs. 0.672 vs. 0.628 in the internal validation cohort, and 0.733 vs. 0.671 vs. 0.579 in the external validation cohort. The nomogram integrating DL_RiskScore, Rad-score, and GPA achieved C-index values of 0.809, 0.764 and 0.733 in training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. Conclusions : A DL model based on pre-treatment MRI can effectively predict survival outcomes in patients with BM, offering a potential tool for individualized prognostic risk stratification.

title: Advances in Radiotherapy for Glioblastoma and IDH-Mutant High-Grade Astrocytoma: A Biological and Mechanistic Perspective.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) and IDH-mutant high-grade astrocytoma remain therapeutically challenging. Historical GBM chemoradiation trials reported median overall survival of approximately 15-17 months; contemporary outcomes vary with molecular features, patient selection, and additional therapies. The 60 Gy in 30 fractions partial-brain regimen remains the reference standard for fit patients with newly diagnosed GBM. This narrative review examines radiotherapy based on its underlying biology, distinguishing GBM from IDH-mutant astrocytoma under the WHO molecular framework. It links DNA damage, cell-death programs, and radiation-induced immune signaling to the treatment response and DNA repair, stemness, hypoxia, and the microenvironment to resistance. These mechanisms motivate DNA-damage-response inhibitors, molecularly matched radiosensitizers, and immunotherapy combinations. Tumor treating fields are considered as an adjunctive non-ionizing modality. Proton therapy, FLASH, and MRI-guided adaptive radiotherapy are evaluated for their rationale and normal-tissue effects. Neurocognitive injury is discussed alongside the limitations of proposed hippocampal-sparing objectives. Personalization requires molecular selection and mechanism-matched treatment, with the clinical validation of benefits beyond dosimetry or imaging alone.

title: Does Learning from Unlabeled Data Help Cancer Diagnosis and Prognosis? Semi-Supervised and Self-Supervised Learning Versus Tabular Foundation Model.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Machine learning for cancer diagnosis and prognosis requires costly patient labels. Semi- and self-supervised methods exploit unlabeled data but are rarely tested against equivalent supervised models. We tested whether unlabeled data help and compared these methods with a tabular foundation model. Methods: Four public breast cancer datasets (WDBC, Mammography, METABRIC, SEER) crossed clinical task (diagnosis, including the detection of microcalcifications on Mammography, or prognosis) with class balance. In five-fold cross-validation with five seeds, 10%, 20%, or 50% of training records were labeled. Self-training (random forest and XGBoost), label spreading, and SCARF self-supervised pretraining were each compared with a matched supervised control; logistic regression and TabPFN v2 were references. Analyses used corrected resampled t -tests with Holm adjustment, Bayesian correlated and hierarchical tests, and power analysis. Results: Of 96 comparisons with matched controls in the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC), three were significant, all involving SCARF: two losses on Mammography and one PR-AUC gain on METABRIC that persisted with all labels. The estimated minimum detectable effects at 80% power varied across comparisons, with medians of approximately 0.06 in PR-AUC and 0.09 in MCC; the median absolute observed differences were 0.008 and 0.015, respectively. At the default threshold and 10% labels, label spreading lowered sensitivity on SEER (-0.135) and random-forest self-training on Mammography (-0.122). TabPFN had the highest PR-AUC in all 16 settings. Conclusions: Under the evaluated datasets, methods and settings, no statistically significant additional benefit from unlabeled data beyond shared preprocessing was detected, but the evidence does not establish equivalence; TabPFN achieved the highest PR-AUC in every setting. New methods should be tested against matched controls and tabular foundation models with adequate power.

originalAbstract: Background/Objectives: Machine learning for cancer diagnosis and prognosis requires costly patient labels. Semi- and self-supervised methods exploit unlabeled data but are rarely tested against equivalent supervised models. We tested whether unlabeled data help and compared these methods with a tabular foundation model. Methods: Four public breast cancer datasets (WDBC, Mammography, METABRIC, SEER) crossed clinical task (diagnosis, including the detection of microcalcifications on Mammography, or prognosis) with class balance. In five-fold cross-validation with five seeds, 10%, 20%, or 50% of training records were labeled. Self-training (random forest and XGBoost), label spreading, and SCARF self-supervised pretraining were each compared with a matched supervised control; logistic regression and TabPFN v2 were references. Analyses used corrected resampled t-tests with Holm adjustment, Bayesian correlated and hierarchical tests, and power analysis. Results: Of 96 comparisons with matched controls in the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC), three were significant, all involving SCARF: two losses on Mammography and one PR-AUC gain on METABRIC that persisted with all labels. The estimated minimum detectable effects at 80% power varied across comparisons, with medians of approximately 0.06 in PR-AUC and 0.09 in MCC; the median absolute observed differences were 0.008 and 0.015, respectively. At the default threshold and 10% labels, label spreading lowered sensitivity on SEER (-0.135) and random-forest self-training on Mammography (-0.122). TabPFN had the highest PR-AUC in all 16 settings. Conclusions: Under the evaluated datasets, methods and settings, no statistically significant additional benefit from unlabeled data beyond shared preprocessing was detected, but the evidence does not establish equivalence; TabPFN achieved the highest PR-AUC in every setting. New methods should be tested against matched controls and tabular foundation models with adequate power.

title: Selective Late-Timepoint <sup>68</sup>Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT in Prostate Cancer: A Management-Focused Framework.
abstract: 68 Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT has the most established evidence base among PSMA-targeted imaging agents for prostate cancer and is incorporated into clinical guidelines internationally for initial staging, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) persistence, biochemical recurrence (BCR), and selection for PSMA-directed therapy. Its integration into routine clinical practice reflects established acquisition workflows and consistently high diagnostic performance, including localization of small-volume nodal and distant disease that may be occult on conventional imaging. Imaging is generally performed approximately 60 min after 68 Ga-PSMA-11 administration; however, interest in additional image acquisition at a later timepoint (i.e., late-timepoint imaging) has emerged, with evidence from published studies and real-world experience from centers of excellence supporting feasibility and utility for select clinical scenarios. This additional late (generally 90 min to 3 h) acquisition may improve lesion-to-background contrast or help characterize low-level uptake, indeterminate findings, and suspected recurrence adjacent to physiologic urinary activity. However, improved contrast or lesion detection does not consistently translate into changes in clinical management, supporting selective rather than routine use. In this narrative review, we synthesize published evidence and expert clinical experience to define the potential role of late-timepoint 68 Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT. We position late-timepoint imaging as a selective, management-focused strategy that can provide complementary information when the standard acquisition leaves a clinically actionable question unresolved. The highest-value applications include early BCR with uncertain local-only versus local-plus-regional nodal recurrence, indeterminate pelvic or metastatic uptake, and suspected local recurrence adjacent to physiologic urinary activity. In appropriately selected cases, a late acquisition may be readily integrated into the established PET workflow using the same imaging system and acquisition framework, enabling patient-specific temporal or postvoid information to refine staging and support individualized treatment planning. We propose a management-anchored framework and practical workflow, based on published literature and clinical experience, to support selective, operationally feasible, and patient-centered use.

title: Single-Fraction Stereotactic Radiosurgery for Spontaneous Canine Brain Tumours Under Human Hospital Standards: A Feasibility Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Standard radiotherapy (RT) protocols for spontaneous canine brain tumours, consisting of multiple fractions delivered over several weeks, impose a considerable burden on patients and owners. Single-fraction stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) represents an attractive alternative, but no study has previously reported this approach for canine glioma treatment conducted under human patient clinical and regulatory standards. Methods : Five pet dogs with presumptive glioma diagnosis based on MRI criteria were treated with a single fraction of linac-generated X-rays delivering 10 Gy to the planning target volume, using three to five non-coplanar arcs of a 6 MV beam at the Grenoble Alps University Hospital. Follow-up consisted of clinical exams, MRI and owner-estimated quality of life (QoL) assessment. Five further dogs were treated with a single 15 Gy RT fraction. Three non-irradiated dogs receiving medical management only served as controls. Results : During the first three months after 10 Gy exposure, QoL improved from 7.1 to 8.3 out of 10. Tumour volume reduced by 57% at one month and by 75% at three months post RT, with a reduction observed in all five dogs. Progressive disease was noted at six and nine months after treatment. Two dogs had no evidence of tumour progression at the time of death due to abdominal diseases. Median survival time of dogs receiving 10 or 15 Gy or without irradiation reached 281, 325, and 27 days, respectively ( p < 0.005). A 15 Gy RT fraction led to imaging findings suggestive of radiation-induced injury in four of five dogs at the time of death. Conclusions : Single-fraction hospital SRS is technically feasible, safe, and effective for spontaneous canine glioma when conducted under human clinical and regulatory standards. A single 10 Gy fraction was well tolerated and associated with tumour response, whereas 15 Gy appeared to approach the tolerance limit of the normal brain. Preliminary clinical outcomes are encouraging, but further validation in larger cohorts is required. This canine model provides a reproducible linac-based reference arm for the optimisation and comparative validation of innovative RT modalities, bridging the gap between preclinical rodent studies and human clinical translation.

title: Bone Marrow Biopsy in the PET/CT Era: Its Role in Hodgkin and Common B-Cell Lymphomas: A Contemporary Narrative Review.
abstract: Background: Bone marrow biopsy (BMB) provides histological information that complements whole-body fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG PET/CT). Its clinical value varies across lymphoma subtypes and extends beyond staging. Methods: This narrative review synthesizes the literature identified through PubMed, Scopus and ScienceDirect searches, supplemented by purposively selected guidelines, foundational studies and citation-linked publications. Recent evidence was prioritized, with older studies retained where needed to explain changes in practice. The synthesis distinguishes diagnostic accuracy, stage migration and consequences for patient management. Results: Routine staging BMB can generally be omitted in PET-staged Hodgkin lymphoma and in DLBCL without a management-changing question about discordant or alternative marrow pathology. Marrow assessment remains part of guideline-based evaluation in FL, MCL and nodal or splenic MZL, particularly when localized treatment, unexplained cytopenias or diagnostic classification makes the result consequential. Pooled PET/CT sensitivity for FL marrow involvement was 67% (95% confidence interval, 38-87%). In one MCL cohort, the PET/CT-negative predictive value was 27.8% at a composite marrow involvement prevalence of 78.4%, illustrating the importance of disease prevalence and reference standards. FDG avidity of extra-nodal MZL lesions does not establish reliable detection of marrow infiltration. Aspirate-based ancillary tests can clarify clonal or alternative pathology, while ctDNA, radiomics and PET/MRI remain complementary approaches. Conclusions: Marrow sampling should answer a defined clinical question. Subtype-specific guidance, laboratory abnormalities and the likely consequences of additional tissue information provide the basis for deciding when biopsy is useful.

title: Radiomic Profiling of Tumor Heterogeneity Predicts Treatment Response in High-Risk Hodgkin Lymphoma: Results from the Phase III AHOD0831 Trial.
abstract: Background/Objectives: To determine whether baseline 18F-FDG PET radiomics improves prediction of treatment response in pediatric and adolescent patients with high-risk Hodgkin lymphoma relative to conventional PET-derived biomarkers. Methods: Baseline FDG-PET/CT data from 115 patients enrolled in the multicenter AHOD0831 trial were analyzed. Total metabolic tumor volume (TMTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG) were calculated from aggregate volume of all lesions. Fifty-nine second-order textural radiomic features were extracted using three fixed SUV discretization bin widths (0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 SUV). Features were selected using univariable testing, correlation-based redundancy reduction, and repeated bootstrapped subsequent least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Logistic-regression models based on selected radiomic features, radiomic features plus TMTV, and conventional PET biomarkers were evaluated using repeated five-fold cross-validation, receiver-operating-characteristic analysis, and decision-curve analysis. Results: Of 115 patients, 54 (47.0%) achieved complete response, while 61 (53.0%) had partial response or stable disease. A core group of heterogeneity-related radiomic features-including gray-level co-occurrence matrix-based informational measures of correlation, gray-level dependence matrix-based gray-level non-uniformity, and neighboring gray tone difference matrix-based coarseness and strength-was retained across discretization schemes. Repeated LASSO resampling identified a limited subset of stable predictors. Across all datasets, radiomics-only models and hybrid models combining radiomic features with TMTV consistently outperformed conventional models based on TMTV and TMTV plus TLG. Exploratory decision-curve analysis suggested greater estimated net benefit for the best-performing radiomics model than for TMTV alone within a potentially clinically relevant threshold-probability range. Conclusions: Baseline FDG-PET radiomics captures intratumoral metabolic heterogeneity and may improve treatment-response prediction in high-risk Hodgkin lymphoma beyond conventional PET-derived biomarkers. These findings warrant independent external validation to determine whether baseline radiomics can improve risk stratification and inform future response-adapted treatment strategies.

title: Re-Evaluating the Cambridge Prognostic Groups for Classification of Non-Metastatic Prostate Cancer Using MRI-Based Disease Characterisation.
abstract: Background: The Cambridge Prognostic Groups (CPG) is a validated prognostic stratification system for prostate cancer mortality (PCM) that is endorsed by national guidelines. The CPG classification, however, was designed using clinical staging and before the advent of contemporary MRI-diagnosed prostate cancer cohorts. Here, we explored the impact of using staging information from pre-biopsy MRI in the CPG classification. Methods: Men with non-metastatic prostate cancer investigated through an MRI-informed biopsy pathway were recruited into a single-centre clinical database. All had an upfront multiparametric MRI, which was used to assign T stage and guide biopsies. Other data variables collected included age, diagnostic PSA, Grade Group (GG), biopsy details, and MRI visibility (Likert) scores. Firth-penalized Cox proportional hazards, survival curves, competing risk-regression and concordance index were used to test for the primary outcome of PCM and for progression to metastasis. Results: Data from 1231 men with a median follow-up of 8.8 years were analysed. The median age was 67 years and the median PSA was 7.7 ng/ml. At pre-biopsy MRI, the majority (>77%) had a visible lesion (Likert ≥ 3). Over the period of follow-up, 61 men progressed to metastasis, 22 died of PCM and 87 died from other causes. In this cohort, the MRI-adapted CPG classification demonstrated strong discrimination for PCM (C-index = 0.82, p < 0.001). Competing-risks analysis also demonstrated a stepwise increase in mortality events with progressively higher CPGs ( p = 0.0003). CPG further demonstrated good discriminative ability for metastatic progression, (C-Index= 0.76, p < 0.001). Competing-risks analysis again showed a stepwise increase in metastatic events with higher CPG groups ( p < 0.001). As a benchmark, we also assessed using MRI staging in other classification systems: the six-tier NCCN criteria (C-index = 0.78), CAPRA biopsy-based criteria (C-index = 0.78) and four-tier EAU risk groups (C-index = 0.76) for predicting PCM. Prediction of metastatic progression was comparable between the four classification systems. MRI Likert score was not an independent predictor of PCM and adding it to the CPG classification did not appear to improve model discrimination for PCM or for metastatic progression. Conclusions: In this study, the CPG criteria using MRI staging for classifying prostate cancer appear to show good discrimination for disease mortality and metastatic progression.

Competing-risks analysis also demonstrated a stepwise increase in mortality events with progressively higher CPGs (p = 0.0003). CPG further demonstrated good discriminative ability for metastatic progression, (C-Index= 0.76, p < 0.001). Competing-risks analysis again showed a stepwise increase in metastatic events with higher CPG groups (p < 0.001). As a benchmark, we also assessed using MRI staging in other classification systems: the six-tier NCCN criteria (C-index = 0.78), CAPRA biopsy-based criteria (C-index = 0.78) and four-tier EAU risk groups (C-index = 0.76) for predicting PCM. Prediction of metastatic progression was comparable between the four classification systems. MRI Likert score was not an independent predictor of PCM and adding it to the CPG classification did not appear to improve model discrimination for PCM or for metastatic progression. Conclusions: In this study, the CPG criteria using MRI staging for classifying prostate cancer appear to show good discrimination for disease mortality and metastatic progression.

title: Ichthammol and Sodium Bituminosulfonate for Retinal Neuroprotection: Molecular Rationale, Translational Barriers and Ocular Safety of an Untested Hypothesis.
abstract: Age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, and inherited retinal dystrophies share a final common pathway of chronic low-grade inflammation, oxidative stress, and progressive loss of photoreceptors, retinal pigment epithelium, and inner retinal neurons, and the inflamed microenvironment of the degenerating retina is a major obstacle to cell-based therapies. Sulfonated shale oils-ammonium bituminosulfonate (ichthammol) and sodium bituminosulfonate, marketed since 1882 under the trade name Ichthyol-have been used topically in dermatology for more than a century and inhibit, in leukocytes, macrophages, and cell-free assays, several mediators that also drive retinal degeneration: 5-lipoxygenase and leukotriene B 4 synthesis, the phagocyte oxidative burst, matrix metalloproteinase 9, and neutrophil release of elastase and vascular endothelial growth factor. This hypothesis-generating review asks whether this pharmacology could be relevant to the posterior segment and states at the outset what the evidence does not contain: no study of bituminosulfonates has ever been performed in retinal cells, retinal tissue, animal models of retinal disease, patients with retinal disease, or any neural tissue; no ocular pharmacokinetic or toxicological data exist; and product labels and safety data sheets classify these preparations as eye irritants for external use only, not to be used in the eye. Their historical ophthalmic use was confined to eyelid skin. Within these constraints, we map the non-ocular mechanisms of bituminosulfonates onto retinal pathobiology and onto the obstacles of retinal cell therapy, compare them with repurposed anti-inflammatory agents already tested in retinal trials, and examine the biological differences between skin and retina and the pharmacokinetic barriers to retinal exposure. We conclude that retinal toxicity, rather than efficacy, is the first question to be answered, and we propose a stepwise, go/no-go preclinical program-from retinal cell cultures to organoids, explants, and animal models-whose negative outcome at any stage would close the hypothesis. No clinical use of bituminosulfonates in or near the posterior segment is suggested by this article.

title: CT-Defined Injury Patterns and 90-Day Functional Status After Operative Pediatric Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: Background/objectives Children who require surgery after traumatic brain injury (TBI) represent a heterogeneous population. We compared 90-day functional status between epidural hematoma (EDH)-predominant injuries and injuries containing acute subdural hematoma (SDH) and/or cerebral contusion, and examined whether quantitative CT measures added useful context. Methods We retrospectively studied 53 patients aged 1-18 years who underwent cranial surgery for acute TBI between June 2020 and June 2026. The primary comparison included 41 patients aged ≤ 16 years; 40 (97.6%) had assigned 90-day Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended Pediatric Revision (GOS-E Peds) status. Preoperative CT scans were reviewed using a predefined protocol. Results SDH/contusion-associated patients had lower admission GCS (median 10 vs. 15) and higher Rotterdam CT scores (3 vs. 1). Good recovery (GOS-E Peds 1-2) at 90 days occurred in 9/13 (69.2%) SDH/contusion-associated patients and 25/27 (92.6%) EDH-predominant patients. The corresponding exact odds ratio for absence of good recovery was 5.28 (95% CI 0.63-68.02; p = 0.075), with an absolute risk difference of +23.4 percentage points (95% CI -0.8 to 50.8). Adjustment for admission GCS attenuated the association (OR 2.57, 95% CI 0.37-19.09). Continuous midline shift was similar between the CT-pattern groups and was not associated with 90-day status. Conclusions CT-defined injury patterns identified children with different initial injury burdens, but the 90-day association was imprecise and partly tracked admission neurological severity. CT anatomy should therefore be interpreted together with the clinical examination rather than used as a stand-alone prognostic classifier.

title: Role of Functional Luminal Imaging Probe in the Evaluation and Management of Pediatric Esophageal Disorders.
abstract: Assessment of esophageal function in pediatric populations remains challenging due to the limited biomechanical information provided by conventional diagnostic modalities. While upper endoscopy evaluates mucosal pathology, contrast radiography assesses anatomical features, and high-resolution manometry characterizes pressure dynamics and motility, these techniques do not directly measure esophageal compliance, distensibility, or wall stiffness. These biomechanical properties are increasingly acknowledged as critical determinants of symptom generation and disease progression. The functional luminal imaging probe (FLIP), commercially known as the endoluminal functional lumen imaging probe (EndoFLIP), utilizes impedance planimetry to measure luminal geometry and intrabag pressure during controlled distension. This method allows for the assessment of esophageal diameter, cross-sectional area, distensibility index, and contractile responses. Over the past decade, EndoFLIP has become an important adjunct in evaluating pediatric esophageal disorders, including achalasia, esophagogastric junction outflow obstruction, eosinophilic esophagitis, and other motility disorders. The advent of FLIP panometry has further expanded its utility by providing insights into distension-induced esophageal contractility. Its intraoperative application during peroral endoscopic myotomy and laparoscopic Heller myotomy has enabled real-time assessment of therapeutic effectiveness. However, current pediatric evidence is limited by small sample sizes, predominantly retrospective, single-center study designs, heterogeneous procedural protocols, and insufficient long-term outcome data. In addition, age-appropriate normative values, diagnostic thresholds, and therapeutic targets remain inadequately validated. This review examines the principles of EndoFLIP technology, its current pediatric applications, comparisons with high-resolution manometry, technical challenges, and future prospects. Available evidence suggests that EndoFLIP provides clinically valuable information that complements traditional diagnostic approaches and may increasingly inform the evaluation and management of pediatric esophageal disorders.

title: Automated Trimodal Deep Learning Fusion of MRI, CT, and Endoscopy for Preoperative Differentiation of Sinonasal Inverted Papilloma and Malignant Transformation.
abstract: Purpose: To develop and validate an automated trimodal deep learning fusion framework integrating magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and nasal endoscopy for preoperative differentiation between sinonasal inverted papilloma (SIP) and SIP-transformed squamous cell carcinoma (SIP-SCC). Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 849 patients with pathological diagnoses of SIP ( n = 614) or SIP-SCC ( n = 235) between October 2014 and August 2025. Three unimodal ResNet-based deep learning models were trained and validated using data from 743 patients with only one or two modalities. The trained networks then generated MRI, CT, and endoscopy probability scores for each of 106 separate patients with complete trimodal data. These scores were combined using logistic regression, with fusion performance assessed by five-fold cross-validation in the 106-patient cohort. In the reader study, its performance was compared with six physicians (three junior, three senior). Results: The trimodal fusion model achieved an out-of-fold AUC of 0.910. Its AUC was higher than that of CT (0.634; unadjusted p < 0.001; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and endoscopy (0.813; unadjusted p = 0.023; Holm-adjusted p = 0.045), but the difference from MRI (0.859; unadjusted and adjusted p = 0.142) was not statistically significant. At the fixed threshold of 0.5, the fusion model achieved an accuracy of 83.0%. Accuracy differed significantly between the fusion model and the junior-reader group majority vote (64.2%; unadjusted p = 0.004; adjusted p = 0.022), but not the senior-reader group majority vote (81.1%; unadjusted p = 0.860; adjusted p = 1.000). Conclusions: By integrating MRI, CT, and endoscopy images, the trimodal fusion model achieved the highest AUC among the evaluated models for differentiating SIP from SIP-SCC, suggesting its potential value as a clinical decision support tool.

title: Transforming Stereotactic Radiosurgery with Artificial Intelligence: Toward Intelligent Planning and Streamlined Workflows.
abstract: Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and hypofractionated stereotactic radiotherapy (hSRT) have become a cornerstone in the management of intracranial lesions, offering high precision and ablative dose delivery in one or a limited number of treatment fractions. As clinical indications continue to expand, patients are increasingly treated for larger numbers of brain metastases in a single course and repeat SRS/hSRT courses for new and/or recurrent lesions have become more common. These evolving treatment paradigms substantially increase planning complexity, as target delineation, cumulative dose assessment, normal tissue sparing, and treatment optimization become increasingly challenging with each additional lesion and prior course of radiation. Despite its clinical success, SRS/hSRT treatment planning and delivery remain resource-intensive, requiring expert-driven target and normal structure contouring, treatment plan optimization, and rigorous quality assurance. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) present an opportunity to enhance the efficiency, consistency, and patient-specific personalization of SRS/hSRT workflows while enabling the safe and scalable implementation of increasingly complex clinical applications. This review examines the current and emerging applications of AI across the entire SRS/hSRT treatment delivery pipeline, including automated image segmentation, delineation of targets and normal tissues, treatment planning, and dose prediction. Additionally, we will explore AI-enabled workflow integration and clinical decision support systems that facilitate multidisciplinary collaboration. Challenges to widespread adoption, such as data inhomogeneity, model interpretability, regulatory considerations, and the need for clinical validation, will also be explored. By summarizing current evidence and identifying key research directions, this review outlines a path toward intelligent, streamlined SRS/hSRT workflows in which AI augments clinical expertise and ultimately improves patient outcomes.

title: An Unexpected Twist: Lower Lobe Torsion After Left Upper Lobectomy-A Case Report.
abstract: Lower lobe torsion after lobectomy is a rare complication, and torsion of the left lower lobe after a left upper lobectomy is rarer still. We describe a 69-year-old man with left upper lobe adenocarcinoma who, after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, negative mediastinoscopy samples, and a negative intraoperative frozen section of the aortopulmonary window node, underwent robotic left upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection. On postoperative day 3, chest radiography showed left lower lobe opacification, and computed tomography and bronchoscopy confirmed torsion with complete bronchial occlusion, and thoracotomy confirmed torsion. Emergent thoracotomy revealed a twisted, ischemic lower lobe, which was detorsed and secured to the diaphragm. The lobe remained congested, and follow-up CT showed evolving necrosis and a loculated pleural collection prompting completion pneumonectomy. He remains without evidence of recurrence at 26 months. Persistent congestion after detorsion warrants concern for incomplete recovery of lobar perfusion despite initial clinical stability.

title: Eosinophilic, Polymorphic, and Pruritic Eruption After Pelvic Radiotherapy for Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Eosinophilic, polymorphic, and pruritic eruption associated with radiotherapy (EPPER) is a rare and probably underrecognized cutaneous reaction to ionizing radiation with marked clinicopathological variability. We report a 59-year-old patient with prostate adenocarcinoma who developed a rapidly progressive, generalized pruritic eruption with tense bullae approximately two weeks after initiation of pelvic radiotherapy. The eruption began in the gluteal region and spread to the trunk and extremities, accompanied by shallow buccal erosions and mild systemic inflammation. Diagnostic evaluation showed no evidence of an autoimmune blistering disorder. Histopathology revealed an eosinophil-rich spongiotic dermatitis with vesiculobullous changes, supporting EPPER in the appropriate clinical context. With continued systemic and topical corticosteroid therapy, the eruption gradually resolved. Radiotherapy was temporarily interrupted but subsequently resumed and completed under corticosteroid treatment, with only a mild self-limited flare and no recurrent bullae. This case highlights the vesiculobullous spectrum of EPPER and underscores the importance of the temporal relationship to radiotherapy and close clinicopathological correlation for accurate diagnosis.

title: Metachronous Gastric Metastasis of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Mimicking Early Gastric Cancer and Detected on Esophagogastroduodenoscopy: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Background : Although extrahepatic metastasis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is common in the lungs and bones, metachronous gastric metastasis of HCC, which is initially detected in the form of multiple small gastric polyps, is extremely rare. Case presentation: A 62-year-old man was diagnosed with HCC by abdominal computed tomography (CT), but the patient received only intermittent treatment. After 15 months, esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed multiple 0.3-0.6 cm sessile polyps in the midbody and distal body of the stomach; these findings were not documented in the report of the previous examination. Microscopically, the stomach biopsy specimen revealed tumor cells with prominent nuclear atypia arranged in trabecular and solid patterns and infiltrating the gastric mucosa. However, no signs of glandular intraepithelial neoplasia were found in the gastric mucosa. Immunohistochemically, the tumor was positive for HepPar-1 and glypican-3 and negative for SALL4, cytokeratin-7, and cytokeratin-20, consistent with the immunophenotype of the primary HCC. Therefore, the gastric polyps were diagnosed as metachronous gastric metastasis of HCC. The patient was administered sorafenib, but follow-up CT showed radiological disease progression. He died 3 months after being diagnosed with metachronous gastric metastasis of HCC. Conclusions : Based on our experience, this rare case might help clinicians and pathologists avoid misdiagnosing gastric metastasis of HCC as primary gastric adenocarcinoma with hepatoid differentiation and prevent inappropriate treatment. In patients with HCC, biopsy of newly detected gastric polyps should be considered even when they appear benign on endoscopy, to exclude metastatic involvement.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Artificial Intelligence for the Detection and Segmentation of Periapical Lesions on Cone-Beam Computed Tomography: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) improves periapical lesion detection, but its interpretation is expertise-dependent. This systematic review evaluated artificial intelligence (AI) for detecting, classifying, and segmenting periapical lesions on CBCT. Methods : PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched to 12 December 2025 (PROSPERO: CRD420251184440). Studies comparing AI with an expert- or annotation-based reference standard on human CBCT scans were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed with the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool, and certainty of evidence with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled with a bivariate model where complete 2 × 2 data were available, and all metrics with univariate random-effects models. Results : Eighteen studies were included (detection or classification, 16; segmentation, 6); 15 had unclear risk of bias in at least one domain, and most were retrospective and internally validated. In the bivariate model (seven studies), sensitivity was 88.2% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 77.6-94.2%) and specificity 85.1% (73.4-92.1%). Univariate pooled sensitivity was 90.9% (84.2-94.9%; 14 studies), specificity 89.7% (83.2-93.9%; 11 studies), accuracy 86.7% (78.9-92.0%; 10 studies), and F1-score 83.7% (76.4-89.1%; seven studies). The pooled lesion Dice similarity coefficient was 0.70 (0.61-0.78; six studies), indicating moderate spatial overlap with reference annotations. Heterogeneity was considerable for detection metrics (I 2 = 90-96%), prediction intervals were wide (sensitivity 48-99%), and the certainty of evidence was very low. Conclusions : AI shows promising performance for CBCT-based periapical lesion detection under research conditions, whereas segmentation overlap is moderate. Equivalence to clinicians and clinical effectiveness are not established; prospective, externally validated studies with standardized reference standards are needed.

title: FetalSegNet: Automatic Segmentation of the Fetus and Sub-Anatomical Structures in Prenatal Ultrasound Images Using Hybrid Deep Learning Models.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Automatic segmentation of fetal anatomical structures in prenatal ultrasound images is challenging because of low tissue contrast, noise caused by speckles, anatomical variability and the fact that structures are only partially visible within individual image frames. This study has developed and evaluated FetalSegNet, a multi-label deep learning framework that can simultaneously perform segmentation of the fetus and selected sub-anatomical structures, including the head, arms, legs and heart. Methods : A dataset comprising 3321 prenatal ultrasound images obtained from 217 patients was created, with pixel-level annotations generated under expert supervision. FetalSegNet was implemented using four hybrid encoder-decoder configurations that combine EfficientNetV2-M and MaxViT-S encoders with UNet++ and Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) decoders. Performance was evaluated on an unseen test set using Dice score, intersection over union (IoU), precision, recall, 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD 95 ) and average symmetric surface distance (ASSD). The presence of anatomical structures was also assessed using classification metrics, while HiResCAM was used to examine the spatial relevance of model activations. Results : Among the FetalSegNet configurations, the EfficientNetV2-M-UNet++ model achieved the highest overall segmentation performance, with a Dice (DSC) score of 0.9232, IoU of 0.8746, HD 95 of 4.23 mm, and ASSD of 1.02 mm. Class-specific results indicated better performance in segmentation for the head and fetus, whereas the leg and heart classes showed comparatively poorer and more inconsistent results. The models also achieved high F1-scores and a high level of accuracy in assessing the presence of anatomical structures. HiResCAM analyses showed that model activations were predominantly concentrated within the corresponding anatomical regions. Conclusions : FetalSegNet provides a unified, multi-label framework for simultaneously segmenting the fetus and multiple sub-anatomical structures in prenatal ultrasound images. By combining a hybrid deep-learning architecture with independent output-mask channels, comprehensive boundary-based evaluation, and activation-based interpretability analysis, the framework offers an integrated strategy for fetal anatomical segmentation. These findings support further investigation of FetalSegNet for automated and interpretable analysis of prenatal ultrasound images.

title: The Effect of the Prognostic Nutritional Index and Triglyceride-Glucose Index for Predicting Mortality in Patients with Stroke.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Stroke is an acute condition in which impaired cerebral perfusion causes focal or global neurological dysfunction. Serious complications are a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in patients with stroke. Malnutrition is common in this population, and nutritional markers, including the prognostic nutritional index (PNI), may be useful for early risk assessment of stroke-associated infections. Insulin resistance (IR) is also an emerging risk factor for stroke and has been associated with poor prognosis through various metabolic and inflammatory pathways. The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index has been proposed as a reliable surrogate marker of IR. Various biochemical and clinical parameters are used to assess prognosis in patients with stroke. We investigated the prognostic value of the TyG index and PNI for mortality and early mortality, defined as death within the first 30 days, in these patients. Methods: After application of the exclusion criteria, 415 patients with stroke were included. Demographic characteristics, including age and sex, and comorbidities were reviewed. Complete blood count, biochemical parameters, C-reactive protein, blood gas measurements, and lactate levels were recorded. Brain computed tomography and diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging findings were reviewed to classify patients into ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke subgroups. Patients were grouped as survivors or nonsurvivors, and deaths within the first 30 days were classified as early mortality. PNI and TyG index values were calculated using the following formulas: PNI = 10 × serum albumin (g/dL) + 0.005 × total lymphocyte count (cells/mm 3 ); TyG index = ln [fasting triglycerides (mg/dL) × fasting blood glucose (mg/dL)/2]. Results: Of the 415 patients included, 389 (93.7%) had ischemic stroke and 26 (6.3%) had hemorrhagic stroke. The median age was 74 years (IQR, 65.0-81.0), and the sex distribution was balanced: 207 patients (49.9%) were women and 208 (50.1%) were men. The PNI was lower in nonsurvivors than in survivors in the overall stroke cohort (ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke combined; 40.86 ± 8.02 vs. 46.88 ± 6.85, p < 0.001), the ischemic stroke subgroup (41.12 ± 8.77 vs. 46.82 ± 6.83, p = 0.001), and the hemorrhagic stroke subgroup (39.79 ± 3.79 vs. 48.17 ± 7.32, p = 0.006). The PNI was also lower in patients who died within the first 30 days than in survivors in the overall cohort (41.86 ± 8.42 vs. 46.88 ± 6.85, p < 0.001), the ischemic stroke subgroup (42.46 ± 8.90 vs. 46.82 ± 6.83, p = 0.002), and the hemorrhagic stroke subgroup (38.60 ± 4.35 vs. 48.17 ± 7.32, p = 0.012). Conclusions: Biomarkers calculated using simple hematological parameters have a significant impact on mortality and early mortality in stroke patients (both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke). When we examined the effects of these TyG and PNI markers on mortality in stroke patients in our study, we observed that the PNI had a significant impact on mortality. Although our findings suggest that the PNI independently predicts mortality or could guide risk assessment in the emergency department, we consider this an exploratory observation, as stroke severity measures-such as the NIHSS-and relevant treatment data were not included in our analyses. However, we believe that single-point TyG values do not carry sufficient significance regarding mortality; therefore, future research should take into account cumulative, repeated TyG measurements obtained during patient follow-up.

title: Photon-Counting CT in Oral and Maxillofacial Imaging: Clinical Applications, Dose Efficiency, and Future Perspectives.
abstract: Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) is an emerging imaging technology that combines ultra-high spatial resolution, improved dose efficiency, reduced electronic noise, and intrinsic spectral imaging. These characteristics are particularly relevant to oral and maxillofacial radiology, where accurate depiction of small osseous and dental structures is often required in the presence of metallic restorations or implants. This review summarizes the technical principles of PCCT and examines its current and potential clinical applications across dental and maxillofacial imaging. Available evidence indicates that PCCT can improve visualization of fine root canal anatomy, periodontal and trabecular bone structures, peri-implant interfaces, subtle maxillofacial fractures, and complex sinonasal anatomy. Its spectral capabilities, including virtual monoenergetic imaging and material decomposition, may substantially reduce metal-related artifacts and improve tissue characterization. Early studies also suggest that PCCT can provide high diagnostic image quality at reduced radiation dose, with potential advantages in pediatric imaging and in patients requiring repeated examinations. Beyond morphology, PCCT may support quantitative applications such as bone mineral density assessment, iodine mapping, treatment planning, and the development of imaging biomarkers and artificial intelligence-based analysis. Despite these promising findings, cone-beam CT remains the preferred modality for many routine dental indications because of its accessibility, lower cost, and established clinical workflow. Current evidence for PCCT in oral and maxillofacial radiology is still limited and is largely derived from technical, experimental, and early clinical studies. Further prospective comparisons with cone-beam CT and conventional CT are needed to define task-specific diagnostic benefits, optimized protocols, radiation-dose advantages, and cost-effectiveness. PCCT is therefore best regarded as a promising complementary modality with particular value in diagnostically challenging cases that require very high spatial resolution, spectral information, or effective metal-artifact reduction. Nevertheless, most oral and maxillofacial evidence remains exploratory; improved image-quality metrics should not be equated with superior patient-level diagnostic accuracy. Direct comparisons with optimized CBCT yield heterogeneous, protocol-dependent dose and diagnostic findings. No standardized indication-specific PCCT acquisition framework currently exists for routine oral and maxillofacial imaging. Clinical implementation should therefore be conditional on demonstrable diagnostic benefit at a justified radiation dose and acceptable resource cost.

title: Circulating MicroRNAs in Lung Cancer and Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Diagnostic Potential, Shared Signatures, and Challenges in Differential Diagnosis.
abstract: The differential diagnosis of lung cancer and pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) remains challenging because the diseases share clinical manifestations and radiological features, particularly in regions with a high tuberculosis burden. This narrative review evaluates circulating microRNAs (miRNAs), primarily measured in serum, plasma and extracellular-vesicle-enriched fractions, as potential adjunctive biomarkers for this differential diagnosis. The literature search was updated through 3 October 2026. Evidence was synthesized by comparator group, biological matrix, analytical methodology and validation design, distinguishing direct lung cancer-PTB comparisons from disease-control studies and prognostic or monitoring investigations. Numerous miRNAs have been associated with either disease, but shared candidates and opposite expression directions across separate studies do not establish differential diagnostic accuracy. Findings vary with patient selection, sample processing, detection platforms, normalization and reference standards. Direct blood-based comparisons remain limited and report variable discrimination. A plasma panel comprising miR-342-3p, miR-199a-3p and miR-199b-3p differentiated PTB from lung cancer with areas under the curve of 0.911 in training and 0.886 in internal split-sample validation; validation sensitivity and specificity were 87.9% and 75.9%, respectively. Its case-control design, incomplete microbiological confirmation and absence of concomitant lung cancer-PTB assessment limit clinical interpretation. Additional pleural-fluid findings concern a separate matrix and cannot be extrapolated to blood testing. Prognostic and treatment-associated findings remain exploratory and do not establish treatment-guiding or validated monitoring utility. Circulating miRNAs should therefore be considered potential adjuncts to clinical assessment, imaging, microbiological testing and histopathology. Clinical translation requires standardized assays, independent prospective validation in clinically relevant populations, and demonstration of incremental value and clinical utility within existing diagnostic pathways. Future studies should prespecify intended use, assay procedures and diagnostic thresholds, include patients with coexisting disease, and evaluate whether testing improves clinical decisions without replacing established microbiological or tissue confirmation methods.

title: Admission Prognostic Scores and Endoscopic Findings in Relation to the Two Components of Five-Day Treatment Failure in Acute Variceal Bleeding: An Exploratory Single-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Five-day treatment failure after acute variceal bleeding combines failure of bleeding control and early rebleeding, which may reflect different clinical processes. We explored whether admission scores and endoscopic findings relate similarly to these components. Methods : All 303 consecutive admissions treated with band ligation at a tertiary centre during 2021-2025 were analysed. Six scores were compared using paired AUROCs and Holm adjustment. Results : Failure occurred in 31 admissions (10.2%): 15 failures of primary haemostasis and 17 rebleeds, with one admission meeting both components. Point estimates of discrimination were higher for rebleeding for all six scores (differences 0.123-0.236), but intervals were wide, and no formal between-component test was performed. No comparison among the six scores using the primary score definitions survived the Holm adjustment for the composite or either component; this does not establish equivalence. Active bleeding at endoscopy was associated with failure of primary haemostasis (odds ratio 4.52, 95% CI 1.40-14.53), whereas its association with rebleeding was uncertain (1.07, 0.40-2.90). Red wale markings showed no clear association. Conclusions : This exploratory pattern suggests that the components may capture different clinical processes, a hypothesis requiring prospective confirmation in a larger cohort. Non-standardised outcome classification, uncertain follow-up after transfer, intervening TIPS and sensitivity to recorded versus recomputed scores limit inference.

title: DUET-Net: A Deformable CNN-Transformer with Calibrated Dual Uncertainty for Brain Tumor MRI Classification.
abstract: Background: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a primary modality for brain tumor diagnosis and treatment planning, making accurate automated classification critically important. However, existing deep learning approaches face limitations in prediction reliability, generalization across imaging domains, and calibrated confidence estimation. To address these gaps, we introduce DUET-Net, a hybrid CNN-Transformer framework that integrates six complementary architectural innovations. Methods: First, a multiscale depthwise fusion (MSDF) module aggregates multi-receptive-field context from a single 2D MRI slice using parallel depthwise convolutions at three kernel sizes. Second, domain-adaptive batch normalization (DABN) with input-conditioned mixture weights maintains domain-specific statistics while sharing affine parameters, enabling sample-adaptive generalization across imaging sources. Third, an enhanced convolutional block attention module (CBAM) introduces deformable spatial offsets to adaptively attend to irregular tumor borders. Fourth, a deformable cross-scale attention (DCSA) module combines per-scale learnable spatial offsets with adaptive cross-scale weighting for geometry-aware multi-resolution fusion. Fifth, a hierarchical Vision Transformer encoder coupled with Monte Carlo dropout and a heteroscedastic aleatoric head enables dual uncertainty estimation grounded in the Kendall-Gal framework. Sixth, post-hoc temperature calibration and Grad-CAM++ provide trustworthy confidence scores and visual interpretability. Results: The proposed model achieves 99.51% accuracy on the Kaggle dataset, 95.27% on the Figshare dataset, and 99.89% on the Mendeley dataset with an expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.0142. With approximately 48 M parameters and 6.66 GFLOPs, DUET-Net sustains 52.41 FPS and is the only compared method to provide calibrated uncertainty estimation. Ablation, cross-dataset, and uncertainty-formulation comparison studies further validate the reliability of the framework. Conclusions: The potential of our proposed net as a promising approach for reliable computer-assisted brain tumor classification, although further external and prospective clinical validation is necessary before deployment.

title: Multi-Reference Evaluation of Deep Learning Tumour Segmentation in Multi-Sequence Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma MRI.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Deep learning segmentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is usually reported as one Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) against one reference mask, although multi-sequence MRI is often delineated separately on each sequence. We aimed to quantify how far the choice of reference changes reported performance, and to compare this with the disagreement between radiologists. Methods: We analysed a public dataset of 277 patient records with separately delineated T1-weighted, T2-weighted and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI, 30 of whom were annotated by two radiologists. Tumour volumes were compared without registration. Spatial agreement was measured after rigid registration, with the loss from transferring masks between acquisition grids estimated separately. nnU-Net models were scored against every reference, including the second radiologist's, in 102 held-out patient records. Results: Without registration, the sequence effect on tumour volume was 10.9%, against a reader effect of 5.7% (ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.40 to 2.49). After rigid registration, per-sequence references agreed at a median DSC of 0.783, against 0.898 between radiologists; in the double-annotated patient records, the paired gap narrowed only from 0.129 to 0.083 (95% CI 0.063 to 0.111) when grid transfer was matched. One fixed set of predictions scored 0.726, 0.685 and 0.673, depending only on the reference (median per-patient reference spread 0.075), and switching the reference sequence moved scores 2.7 to 3.6 times as much as switching the radiologist. Conclusions: Part of the cross-sequence difference is a difference in what each sequence makes visible rather than annotation error, so a single-reference DSC on multi-sequence data depends on a rarely stated choice. Performance should be reported against every available reference and read against measured inter-reader agreement.

title: Beyond Conventional MRI: Molecular PET, Multiparametric MRI, and PET/MRI in Glioma Management.
abstract: Despite its central clinical role, conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an incomplete picture of the tumor biology of gliomas, which are biologically heterogeneous tumors. Molecular positron emission tomography (PET) with amino acid tracers, multiparametric MRI techniques (perfusion-, diffusion-, and spectroscopy-based sequences), and hybrid PET/MRI have each been proposed to overcome specific limitations of anatomic imaging in diagnosis, treatment planning, and posttreatment assessment. This narrative review examined the current evidence for molecular PET, multiparametric MRI, and integrated PET/MRI across the glioma care pathway. Rather than framing these modalities as competing alternatives, we argue that amino acid transport, vascularity, water diffusion, and metabolite composition capture distinct and often spatially incongruent facets of tumor biology, such that discordance between modalities may reflect the underlying tumor heterogeneity. We also summarized the guideline recommendations (RANO/EANO, EANM/SNMMI, etc.), outlined current evidence gaps, and discussed emerging directions in novel PET tracers, artificial intelligence, radiomics, and theranostics. Molecular PET and multiparametric MRI should be used as modalities complementary to conventional MRI within multidisciplinary glioma care, while the choice and sequence of examinations should be guided by the clinical question.

title: A 3D CBCT-Based Approach to Assessing Effective Radiation Penetration Depth in Intraoperative Electron Radiotherapy.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Accurate characterization of treatment geometry is essential for intraoperative electron radiotherapy (IOeRT) treatment planning. Mobile cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) enables volumetric assessment of intraoperative anatomy beyond conventional point-based measurements. This study compared clinically applied distance measurement techniques with geometric distance descriptors retrospectively extracted from comprehensive three-dimensional CBCT datasets. Methods : Ninety-six patients receiving IOeRT as a tumor-bed boost during breast-conserving surgery were included. Manual CBCT measurements (mCBCT) were compared with mean (USavg) and minimum (USmin) ultrasound measurements per patient. Comprehensive 3D distance extraction was performed in 82 CBCT datasets using an approximated thoracic-wall surface as the geometric reference. Minimum and first-quartile distances were evaluated across the complete applicator cross-section and within a 1-cm-diameter inner disk around the central beam axis. Results : The mean paired difference between mCBCT and USavg was 0.3 mm and was not statistically significant, whereas mCBCT measurements exceeded USmin by an average of 1.5 mm. In the principal comparison, the minimum CBCT-derived distance within the inner disk was 1.4 mm smaller than mCBCT. Across the complete applicator area, minimum distances were 9.1-10.7 mm smaller than the clinical measurements. The first-quartile distance across all surface points was 1.4 mm smaller than mCBCT, whereas the corresponding inner-disk difference was not statistically significant after correction. Isodose-atlas-based dose-volume analysis indicated that a 1.5-mm change in assumed penetration depth could correspond to an approximately 7% change in the 90% isodose volume at shallow depths. Conclusions : Clinical CBCT and ultrasound measurements showed small group-level differences but substantial patient-level variability. Comprehensive 3D CBCT analysis revealed spatial variations in tissue depth not fully represented by the clinical measurements, highlighting the limitations of characterizing treatment geometry using a single distance. Although anatomical accuracy and patient-specific dosimetric consequences remain to be established, these findings support the potential of intraoperative 3D CBCT to advance IOeRT toward individualized, image-guided treatment planning.

title: Imaging as a Surgical Decision System in Modern Gynecologic Oncology.
abstract: Imaging traditionally supports gynecologic oncology through diagnosis, staging, and estimation of resectability. Contemporary treatment, however, requires longitudinal decisions about which lesion matters, when local intervention is justified, and which modality is proportionate. This critical narrative review proposes imaging as a longitudinal surgical decision system integrating disease trajectory, treatment response, target selection, operative planning, and post-intervention assessment. We define imaging-target mismatch as discordance between the radiologically dominant lesion and the lesion with greatest clinical actionability, and operationalize the disease-modifying surgical window as open, uncertain, or closed across six decision domains. Serial imaging may reveal response-created opportunities, oligopersistence, oligoprogression, competing dissemination, or the need for tissue confirmation, while CT, MRI, ultrasound, and FDG PET/CT provide complementary decision-specific information. Three-dimensional reconstruction, intraoperative imaging, radiomics, and artificial intelligence may enhance planning, but require prospective external validation and should support rather than replace multidisciplinary judgment. Decision-oriented reporting should communicate the target, lesion-level trajectory, competing disease, anatomical feasibility, residual uncertainty, and the relevance of findings to the proposed intervention. Imaging should therefore guide not only what can be treated, but what should be treated, when, and for what therapeutic purpose.

title: Preoperative CT Assessment and Perioperative Decision-Making in Gallbladder Lesions: A Descriptive Pathway Analysis.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Preoperative CT may not reliably distinguish gallbladder malignancy from inflammatory disease, complicating surgical planning. We examined transitions from CT impressions through operative plans, intraoperative reassessment, index procedures, and subsequent treatment. Methods: This retrospective descriptive study screened 651 consecutive patients who underwent gallbladder surgery by a single surgeon at a tertiary referral center from January 2023 to December 2025. The analytic cohort included 41 patients with indeterminate or suspicious CT impressions or malignancy on final pathology. CT categories were assigned from original radiology reports independently of operative intent and pathology. Results: CT impressions were benign in six patients, indeterminate in 11, and suspicious in 24; malignancy was confirmed in six, three, and 16, respectively. Among indeterminate cases, eight had simple cholecystectomy plans, two frozen-guided plans, and one a radical-possible plan; all three malignant cases had conditional oncologic plans. Frozen section was performed in 11 patients, identifying malignancy in nine. Of 19 extended index procedures, 18 were performed under plans allowing oncologic extension; one represented an unanticipated extension. Six patients with T1b or more advanced cancer initially underwent simple cholecystectomy; three subsequently underwent completion surgery. Conclusions: Patients with the same CT impression followed different operative and subsequent management pathways. These findings highlight the clinical importance of considering diagnostic uncertainty throughout the surgical course, from preoperative planning and intraoperative reassessment to subsequent treatment decisions informed by final pathology.

title: MRI Radiomics-Based Nomogram Integrating Skeletal Muscle Assessment for Predicting Pathologic Complete Response to Neoadjuvant Therapy in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.
abstract: Background/Objectives : We aim to develop and internally evaluate a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics-based nomogram integrating clinicopathologic and skeletal muscle measures for predicting pathologic complete response (pCR) in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Methods: This retrospective study included 174 patients with stage II-III TNBC receiving neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy ( n = 94) or chemotherapy alone ( n = 80), followed by surgery. Pretreatment MRI features underwent redundancy reduction and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) selection. Six candidate models combined radiomic, clinicopathologic, and skeletal muscle predictors. Models were fitted using Firth penalized logistic regression. Internal validation used 1000 bootstrap resamples, repeating supervised feature selection, predictor selection, and final-model selection while keeping the 325 radiomic candidates fixed. Area under the curve (AUC), calibration, prediction error, and selection stability were evaluated. Results : Eighty-five patients (48.9%) achieved pCR. Seven radiomic features constituted the score. Corrected AUCs were 0.659 for the clinicopathologic model, 0.622 after adding radiomics, and 0.629 (95% CI: 0.500-0.701) for the fully integrated model (apparent AUC, 0.793). Its corrected Brier score (0.309) exceeded the constant-prevalence benchmark (approximately 0.250). Skeletal muscle density was not independently associated with pCR ( p = 0.130) and did not significantly improve AUC over the radiomics-plus-clinicopathologic model (ΔAUC = 0.009, p = 0.428). The fully integrated model was selected in 50.3% of resamples, while 99.9% of selected models contained radiomic information. Conclusions : The radiomic score showed exploratory associations with pCR, but optimism-corrected performance and model stability were limited. Skeletal muscle density did not significantly improve discrimination. External validation is required before clinical application.

title: Performance Evaluation of Deep Learning Applications in Calcaneal Fracture Diagnosis Using Separate Radiographic Views: A Comparison of CNN and Vision Transformer Architectures.
abstract: Background: Calcaneal fractures are challenging to diagnose on routine radiographs and may result in missed diagnoses. Objective: This study compares Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures for detecting calcaneal fractures separately in three standard radiographic views: Anteroposterior (AP), Harris (axial), and Lateral. Methods: A balanced retrospective dataset of 178 patients with complete three-view examinations (89 with displaced calcaneal fractures and 89 controls) was used to evaluate five deep learning models: ResNet50, InceptionV3, InceptionResNetV2, XCiT, and PiT. After image-quality screening, each view underwent an approximately 8:2 image-level training-validation split; no independent test set was used. Images were preprocessed using data augmentation and Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE), while Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was employed to visualize model activation. Results: InceptionV3 achieved 100% sensitivity in the AP view, while ResNet50 achieved 100% specificity in both AP and Lateral views. XCiT matched ResNet50 across all five classification metrics in the AP view and matched ResNet50 and InceptionV3 in the Lateral view. PiT achieved 100% accuracy in the Harris validation set (95% CI, 89.0-100.0%). Grad-CAM visualizations showed activation over the calcaneal region in representative fracture images. Conclusions: This study demonstrates the feasibility of deep learning for identifying displaced calcaneal fractures through separate evaluations of AP, Harris, and Lateral radiographs. The model-specific performance patterns provide a foundation for further development of AI-assisted calcaneal fracture detection and future investigation of multi-view integration.

title: AI-Supported Semiquantitative CT Characterization of COVID-19 Pneumonia Across SARS-CoV-2 Wild-Type, Alpha, and Delta Variants and Its Association with Clinical Parameters.
abstract: Objective: An AI-based software prototype for the detection of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pneumonia was evaluated regarding its potential to quantify pulmonary opacities across Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) variant groups, incorporating clinical and radiological parameters to facilitate faster diagnosis and therapy. Methods: Chest computed tomography (CT) examinations of 255 patients with confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia were analyzed using an AI-supported semiquantitative CT software prototype between November 2020 and December 2021. The results were correlated with clinical and laboratory parameters. The cohort consisted of wild-type ( n = 93), Alpha ( n = 66), Beta/Gamma ( n = 3), and Delta ( n = 93). Beta/Gamma cases were excluded from subgroup comparisons due to the small number of patients. Results: The mean AI-derived COVID-19 probability was 0.84 ± 0.33. After exclusion of five technically non-evaluable measurements, global mean opacity attenuation differed significantly among the wild-type (-475.12 ± 116.47 Hounsfield Units (HU)), Alpha (-464.68 ± 114.80 HU), and Delta groups (-423.92 ± 112.56 HU; Kruskal-Wallis H(2) = 12.062, p = 0.002). The Volume of Opacity showed no significant differences between wild-type (984.64 ± 908.92 mL), Alpha (1161.17 ± 933.55 mL), and Delta (988.19 ± 866.20 mL) ( p = 0.339). The extent of pulmonary involvement (Volume of Opacity) correlated with the duration of hospital stay (r = 0.311, p < 0.001**), duration of intensive care treatment (r = 0.468, p < 0.001**), and the laboratory parameters CRP, leukocyte count, relative lymphocyte count, and AST ( p < 0.001**). It showed no significant correlation with the duration of invasive ventilation ( p > 0.05). A total of 37 (14.5%) patients died and 92 (36.1%) required intensive care unit (ICU) admission. Manual corrections of lung lobe and infiltrate boundaries were performed in 221/255 datasets and were required in all assessed datasets (221/221, 100%). Conclusions: The CT Pneumonia Analysis Prototype enabled semiquantitative assessment of pulmonary opacities across different SARS-CoV-2 variants but required radiological oversight and manual correction of the automated segmentations. Given the retrospective observational design, the findings should be interpreted in light of potential confounding and heterogeneity in CT acquisition protocols. The observed associations suggest that combining semiquantitative CT parameters with clinical and laboratory data may be of potential relevance for future prognostic models, which requires further evaluation in multivariable analyses.

title: Reproducibility Before Treatment Decision Rules: A Targeted Scoping Review of AI-Assisted Coronary Plaque Characterization.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) can quantify plaque, whose burden predicts myocardial infarction better than stenosis severity. We reviewed evidence for artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted plaque characterization. Methods: This targeted scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) used a non-exhaustive search, mainly of MEDLINE/PubMed (July 2026, supplemented in September). AI title selection (135 of 1415 titles) and author assessment of 141 records yielded 121 included records under the revised criteria. An AI re-screen of 1280 unselected records (blind second pass on 175) found 110 further eligible records after charting; two AI passes screened 3634 confirmatory records (κ 0.93). The corresponding author accepted AI recommendations after reviewing written assessments, not blind (for the 335 confirmatory records, in one instruction). Of the 543 eligible records, 236 were charted (121 + 110 + 4 + 1; full text for 121 of the 236, abstract alone for 115) and 307 mapped from abstracts only (not fully charted). Results: In symptomatic or referred patients, AI-derived plaque burden was associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (a property of the measurement, not evidence that AI improves outcomes). In one comparison, AI modestly improved discrimination over manual quantification (AUC 0.82 vs. 0.78) without significant net reclassification improvement. No randomized trial of AI-based plaque analysis reporting clinical endpoints was identified in the sources searched and assessed; TRANSFORM (NCT06112418) is recruiting. Three small same-patient comparisons found systematic between-platform differences; no adequately powered comparison of major commercial platforms was identified. Abstract-level mapping of the 307 additional records identified no randomized outcome, observed decision-impact or photon-counting prognostic study. Conclusions: AI-derived plaque measures carry prognostic information in symptomatic patients, but randomized evidence that AI-guided treatment reduces myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death in asymptomatic adults, or does so better than coronary artery calcium (CAC)-guided prevention, has not been established in the sources searched and assessed. Under the modeled effects, demonstrating benefit in the lowest-burden stage would need an impractically large trial; as a design proposal, we outline a stage-enriched randomized trial. AI-assisted plaque characterization is best understood as a throughput and within-system repeatability technology; cross-platform portability is not demonstrated, and it is not a validated treatment decision rule.

title: Anatomical Validity of MRI-Based Choroid Plexus Segmentation: Regional Boundaries, Age-Related Morphology, and Implications for Neuroimaging Biomarkers.
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived choroid plexus (ChP) volume is increasingly investigated in studies of brain aging and neurodegeneration, yet its anatomical meaning remains uncertain because segmentation methods differ in ventricular coverage, image contrast, and reference annotations. This narrative review examines the anatomical basis and methodological validity of ChP volumetry by integrating evidence on ventricular anatomy, age-related tissue changes, manual and automated segmentation, and associations with cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease. The lateral ventricular ChP, particularly the atrial glomus, is generally easier to delineate on conventional MRI than its thin extensions and the third and fourth ventricular components. Segmentation performance depends on the anatomical reference and acquisition protocol; agreement with manually drawn masks does not necessarily establish complete anatomical coverage. In addition, age-related vascular remodeling, changes in stromal composition, calcification, and cystic alterations can affect MRI appearance and the interpretation of total volume. Although ChP enlargement has been associated with aging, cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease, volume alone cannot identify the contributing tissue compartments or establish blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier dysfunction. We propose an anatomy-centered approach to ChP volumetry based on explicit regional definitions, complementary measures of spatial and volumetric accuracy, assessment of test-retest and multicenter reliability, and independent biological validation when functional interpretations are intended.
