title: Regorafenib-Associated Pancreatic Atrophy and Survival Outcomes in Metastatic Colorectal Cancer.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Regorafenib is a multikinase inhibitor approved for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). VEGF-pathway inhibition may also cause structural changes in normal organs, including pancreatic volume loss. We evaluated pancreatic volume changes during regorafenib therapy and their association with treatment exposure and clinical outcomes. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 85 of 115 screened patients with mCRC treated with regorafenib at a single center who had contrast-enhanced CT before treatment and at the first response evaluation. Pancreatic atrophy was defined a priori as a ≥10% volume reduction from baseline. Survival was analyzed with a 12-week landmark approach; for OS, landmark and time-dependent Cox models were added. Results: Median pancreatic volume decreased from 54.22 to 50.00 mL (median paired change -5.8%, 95% CI -9.1 to -4.2; p < 0.001), and atrophy developed in 31 patients (36.5%). Atrophy was associated with longer treatment duration (median 149 vs. 92 days; p = 0.001) and higher disease control (58.6% vs. 17.3%; p < 0.001). The conventional PFS comparison favored the atrophy group (5.26 vs. 3.29 months; p = 0.003) but is confounded by guarantee-time bias. In the 12-week landmark population ( n = 65), median PFS was 2.50 vs. 1.28 months (log-rank p = 0.046); however, atrophy was not independently associated with PFS (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.39-1.20; p = 0.181). Median OS was 11.30 vs. 6.74 months ( p = 0.271), and atrophy was not independently associated with OS in conventional (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.60-1.64), landmark (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.62-1.76), or time-dependent (HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.69-1.94) models. Conclusions: Regorafenib-associated pancreatic atrophy is a measurable imaging finding linked to longer treatment exposure and concurrent disease control. After accounting for guarantee-time bias, it was not independently associated with PFS or OS and should not be regarded as a prognostic biomarker.

In the 12-week landmark population (n = 65), median PFS was 2.50 vs. 1.28 months (log-rank p = 0.046); however, atrophy was not independently associated with PFS (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.39-1.20; p = 0.181). Median OS was 11.30 vs. 6.74 months (p = 0.271), and atrophy was not independently associated with OS in conventional (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.60-1.64), landmark (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.62-1.76), or time-dependent (HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.69-1.94) models. Conclusions: Regorafenib-associated pancreatic atrophy is a measurable imaging finding linked to longer treatment exposure and concurrent disease control. After accounting for guarantee-time bias, it was not independently associated with PFS or OS and should not be regarded as a prognostic biomarker.

title: AI-Driven Analysis of Longitudinal MRI Marrow Patterns Predicts Survival in Multiple Myeloma Treatment.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Multiple myeloma (MM) remains incurable, with most patients eventually experiencing relapse/progression despite advances in treatment. This preliminary study evaluated the prognostic value of longitudinal changes in vertebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) patterns using a two-stage machine learning (2S-ML) framework. Methods : The study included 62 patients with paired spinal MRI scans acquired before and after autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT). First, a pre-trained ResNet-18 was fine-tuned to classify vertebrae into four marrow infiltration patterns. Second, 12 handcrafted temporal descriptors were extracted to characterize longitudinal changes in MRI patterns. Ridge-penalized Cox proportional hazards regression was employed as the primary model to predict time to progression (TTP) and overall survival (OS). A random forest classifier was retained as a secondary analysis for fixed-horizon outcome prediction, and model performance was evaluated using patient-level leave-one-case-out cross-validation (LOCO-CV). Results : The 4MRI-P model achieved an average AUC of 0.8905 ± 0.0054 across 1208 vertebral MRI annotations. In the primary Cox analysis, adding longitudinal MRI features to clinical variables modestly improved the C-index for TTP (0.6950 to 0.7301) and OS (0.6801 to 0.6924). The secondary random forest analysis achieved time-dependent AUCs of 0.8291 ± 0.0844 for TTP at 36 months and 0.7396 ± 0.0776 for OS at 60 months. Kaplan-Meier analyses showed significant separation between risk groups for both outcomes (both p < 0.001). Conclusions : These preliminary findings suggest that AI-driven analysis of longitudinal vertebral MRI patterns may provide prognostic value for survival risk stratification in MM.

title: Reassessing the Prognostic Value of the Extent of Resection in the Era of Neoadjuvant Immunotherapy for Glioblastoma.
abstract: Extent of resection (EOR) is an established prognostic factor in glioblastoma (GBM). Neoadjuvant immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) aims to strengthen antitumor immunity before surgery, but its effect on the surgical and radiological variables that define EOR has received little scrutiny. This narrative review examines the four neoadjuvant-ICI trials in GBM. Only one reported resection metrics: presurgical and postsurgical tumor volume, percent resection, and gross total resection did not differ between arms, and none was selected as a survival predictor in an elastic-net regression. The other three trials reported no resection data. No trial tested whether neoadjuvant ICI changes the achievable resection margin, the reliability of the early postoperative MRI used to calculate EOR, or the prognostic value of EOR. Evidence on ICI-associated pseudoprogression concerns later, longitudinal imaging, and the only dedicated GBM cohort found no pseudoprogression attributable to ICI monotherapy. Future neoadjuvant-ICI trials should prespecify EOR as an endpoint using a standardized classification such as RANO resect, standardize postoperative MRI timing, adjudicate the early postoperative scan separately from response-assessment imaging, and include newly diagnosed patients. These gaps should be read against the broader record of immunotherapy in GBM, where checkpoint inhibitors, vaccines, and gene or viral therapies have not yet improved survival in randomized trials.

title: MRI-Based Habitat Radiomics for Predicting Early Recurrence After Pancreatic Cancer Resection.
abstract: Purpose: To investigate the predictive performance of multi-sequence MRI habitat radiomics for early recurrence (ER) following curative resection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and to provide preoperative imaging evidence to guide personalized diagnosis and treatment. Methods: This study collected retrospective clinical data from a total of 260 PDAC patients at two medical centers. Tumors were segmented into three habitat subregions via unsupervised K-means clustering. Radiomic features from these subregions were used to construct the habitat models. The performance of the traditional clinical model, the whole-tumor radiomics model, the single-sequence habitat models, the combined habitat model, and the Clinic-Habitat combined model was compared. The model's validity was evaluated using a series of metrics, including the area under the ROC curve (AUC), calibration curve analysis, and decision curve analysis (DCA). The results of the model were interpreted using the additive interpretation method of SHAP. Spearman's rank-order correlation analysis was performed to explore biological correlations between radiomic scores and pathological markers. Risk-stratified survival analysis was implemented based on model-derived optimal cutoff values. Results: The Clinic-Habitat model demonstrated the best performance, with AUCs of 0.922 (training), 0.896 (internal validation), and 0.886 (external test), outperforming the clinical baseline model, the clinical-pathological model, the individual-sequence habitat models, and the whole-tumor radiomics model. SHAP analysis indicated that T1WI-Hab-score1 exerted the greatest influence on model predictions. The Hab-radiomic score was significantly correlated with pathological markers reflecting tumor aggressiveness. A cutoff value of 0.556 derived from the Clinic-Habitat model effectively stratified patients into high- and low-risk ER subgroups, with Kaplan-Meier curves showing a significant difference in RFS between the two groups ( p < 0.001). Conclusions: Multi-sequence MRI-based habitat radiomics enables preoperative prediction of ER risk in PDAC and facilitates patient risk stratification and personalized treatment planning.

title: Blood Speckle Tracking Echocardiography in Congenital Heart Disease: Current Applications, Emerging Flow Signs, and Future Perspectives: An Opinion Review.
abstract: Blood speckle tracking (BST) echocardiography is an emerging ultrafast ultrasound-based imaging technique that enables visualization of blood-flow patterns in cardiac chambers and great vessels. In the studies reviewed here, acquisition and flow tracking are predominantly performed in two-dimensional imaging planes and across time; therefore, the term "4D" should not be interpreted as a validated, fully volumetric three-dimensional flow acquisition. By exploiting high-frame-rate plane-wave imaging, BST allows angle-independent reconstruction of multidirectional flow vectors, vortex formation, turbulent propagation, and flow energetics, providing hemodynamic information beyond that obtainable with conventional Doppler echocardiography. This capability is particularly relevant in fetuses, neonates, and children with congenital heart disease (CHD), in whom altered chamber geometry, abnormal loading conditions, and complex postoperative anatomies frequently generate non-laminar flow patterns, recirculation zones, and pathological vortices. Over the last few years, studies have reported high feasibility of BST in selected pediatric and fetal populations, with successful acquisition rates exceeding 90% in several cohorts. However, feasibility estimates vary by study, population, imaging plane, and endpoint, and reproducibility and clinical validity remain incompletely established. Current applications include assessment of ventricular vortex morphology, energy loss, intraventricular pressure differences, aortic and pulmonary flow patterns, and characterization of altered hemodynamics in complex CHD, including bicuspid aortic valve disease, tetralogy of Fallot, coarctation of the aorta, cardiomyopathies, and single ventricle physiology. Early studies suggest that BST-derived parameters, such as vorticity, kinetic energy, vector complexity, and pressure gradients, may provide incremental pathophysiological and potentially prognostic information beyond conventional echocardiographic metrics. Despite its promising clinical potential, widespread implementation of BST remains limited by restricted software availability, limited penetration depth, lack of standardized quantitative reference values, and the still limited evidence regarding its diagnostic and prognostic superiority over standard imaging techniques. This review provides an up-to-date overview of the technical principles, current clinical applications, hemodynamic insights, and future perspectives of BST echocardiography in congenital heart disease.

title: Impact of Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging Preprocessing Steps on the DTI-ALPS Index.
abstract: Background/Objectives : The diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index is a non-invasive glymphatic function marker. Derived from the ratio of orthogonal diffusivities, it may be susceptible to systematic bias from diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) preprocessing. This study quantitatively evaluated the effect of individual preprocessing steps on the DTI-ALPS index. Methods : The dMRI and T1-weighted images of 100 cognitively normal participants under an identical protocol were obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Six conditions were derived from identical source data: no preprocessing; four single-step pipelines (denoising, Gibbs ringing correction, eddy current/motion correction, or bias field correction); and full preprocessing. Results : Significant differences in the DTI-ALPS index were observed across preprocessing conditions (χ 2 (5) = 97.947, p < 0.001), with a modest overall effect size (Kendall's W = 0.196). Relative to the no-preprocessing condition, Gibbs ringing correction decreased the index by 0.63% on average (SD of percentage change, 0.72%), while eddy current and motion correction decreased it by 0.31% on average but showed greater interindividual variability (SD, 2.36%). The full preprocessing pipeline resulted in a mean decrease of 0.54%. Denoising and bias field correction produced no significant changes. Thus, despite statistical significance for several preprocessing conditions, the magnitude of the observed changes in the DTI-ALPS index was small. Conclusions : Individual preprocessing steps differentially affect the DTI-ALPS index. Gibbs ringing correction contributed the most consistent effect, while eddy current and motion correction exerted a significant, independent effect. These findings indicate that specific preprocessing steps can introduce statistically detectable but quantitatively small changes in the DTI-ALPS index. Standardized preprocessing may therefore be particularly important for cross-study harmonization, meta-analyses, and longitudinal or serial monitoring, where subtle differences in the DTI-ALPS index may affect comparability.

title: Comparative Ergonomic Assessment of Microscopic, Endoscopic, and RobOtol<sup>®</sup>-Assisted Ear Surgery: A Prospective Pilot Study.
abstract: Background: Otologic surgery imposes prolonged static postures and fine-motor demands on the surgeon, yet the ergonomic effect of robotic endoscope holding is unknown. We compared surgeon-perceived workload, fatigue and workflow during microscopic, conventional endoscopic and RobOtol ® -assisted endoscopic ear surgery. Methods: In this prospective single-center pilot study, one surgeon performed 29 procedures: RobOtol ® (n = 9), conventional endoscopy (n = 10) and microscopy (n = 10). After each procedure, the surgeon rated five NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX)-derived workload domains (0-10; unweighted mean), comfort, neck, eye and hand fatigue, instrument stability and movement precision. Setup time, operative time and repositionings were recorded. Kruskal-Wallis and Holm-adjusted Mann-Whitney U tests were used, with false discovery rate control across secondary outcomes. Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) scores from intraoperative photographs were analyzed descriptively. Results: Modified NASA-TLX scores were 3.58 ± 1.50 (RobOtol ® ), 3.78 ± 1.54 (endoscopy) and 5.52 ± 1.54 (microscopy) ( p = 0.026, ε 2 = 0.26); no pairwise difference remained significant after Holm adjustment. Eye fatigue was higher with microscopy than with either endoscopic approach (adjusted p ≤ 0.016). Compared with conventional endoscopy, RobOtol ® yielded higher surgeon-rated instrument stability (mean difference 2.72, 95% CI 1.79-3.65; adjusted p < 0.001) and movement precision (1.04, 95% CI 0.41-1.67; adjusted p = 0.019) without higher workload. Operative time was longest with microscopy (130.7 vs 76.8 and 77.3 min; p = 0.004). Mean RULA scores were 3.38-3.77 (action level 2) in all groups. Conclusions: Endoscopic approaches were associated with lower perceived workload and eye fatigue than microscopy, and robotic endoscope holding was associated with higher perceived stability and precision without added workload. As case mix differed between groups and outcomes were self-rated, these hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in larger multi-surgeon studies with objective performance and posture measurement.

title: Mammography-Based Artificial Intelligence for Breast Arterial Calcification Detection, Quantification, and Cardiovascular Risk Assessment: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Artificial intelligence (AI) may automate breast arterial calcification (BAC) assessment and extract cardiovascular information from mammograms. In this study, we review technical BAC assessment, computed tomography (CT)-derived coronary artery calcification (CAC) surrogate assessment, and cardiovascular associations and prediction. Methods : MEDLINE and Embase were searched through 29 August 2026, supplemented by citation searching. Reports were synthesized narratively by target task, reference standard, and predictor type. QUADAS-2 and PROBAST informed risk-of-bias assessment. Results : Database screening yielded 17 eligible reports, and citation searching added three, resulting in 20 reports from 19 studies. These included 12 technical BAC reports, two CAC-surrogate reports, and six cardiovascular reports comprising five BAC-specific studies and one whole-mammogram study. BAC-detection areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) reached 0.95-0.96; segmentation Jaccard coefficients were approximately 0.58-0.61, and one small internal validation reported a Dice of 0.89. Mammography-only CAC AUCs ranged from 0.761 to 0.850 across thresholds; an AI-derived BAC score yielded AUC 0.64 for marked CAC. In an external health system cohort, severe versus absent BAC was associated with major adverse cardiovascular events after adjustment for Predicting Risk of cardiovascular disease EVENTs (PREVENT) (hazard ratio 2.80; 95% confidence interval 2.36-3.32). Separately, adding categorical BAC to PREVENT increased the external cohort C-index from 0.62 to 0.64. Conclusions : AI enables automated BAC assessment, and BAC-derived measures show prognostic associations with limited evidence of incremental predictive performance. Whole-mammogram models provide complementary evidence that cannot establish BAC-specific prognostic value. These tasks require separate interpretation. Standardized measurement, external validation, calibration, and prospective evidence of clinical benefit remain necessary.

title: Deep Myometrial Invasion in Superficial Spreading Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Cervix: A Rare Case Report.
abstract: Background : Cervical squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) can spread upward along the endometrial surface, usually without invading the uterine wall, and is difficult to separate from primary endometrial SCC involving the cervix. Case presentation : A 72-year-old woman, treated by conization for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 ten years earlier and lost to follow-up, presented with pelvic pain and a 12 × 8 cm pelvic mass. Without preoperative histology she underwent total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. A poorly differentiated non-keratinizing SCC involved the cervical mucosa with 1 mm of stromal invasion, replaced the endometrium in continuity up to the fundus and invaded 9 mm of the myometrium, more than one-half of its thickness, with focal lymphovascular space invasion. Immunohistochemistry and HPV testing were not performed. The morphology favors a cervical primary with superficial spread (FIGO 2018 stage IA1, since corpus extension is disregarded), but a primary endometrial SCC, which would be staged as endometrial cancer, cannot be excluded. No lymph nodes were examined, and PET/CT showed no residual, nodal or distant disease. The tumor board recommended pelvic radiotherapy (50.4 Gy in 28 fractions), beyond guideline recommendations for stage IA1; PET/CT six months after surgery showed no recurrence. Conclusions : The case illustrates a diagnostic problem. When an SCC replaces the endometrium and invades the myometrium while cervical invasion is minimal, its origin and stage remain uncertain without p16 and HPV testing. Detailed sampling, the explicit reporting of corpus invasion and expert pathology review should precede staging and treatment.

title: Extended Reality-Assisted Exoscopic Cervical Laminoplasty Integrating Intraoperative CT Navigation: A Technical Note on a Surgeon-Centered Virtual Workspace.
abstract: Background/Objectives: In exoscopic spine surgery, the exoscopic image, navigation, and reference imaging occupy separate monitors. We describe a surgeon-centered extended reality (XR) workspace that places these sources in a single consumer head-mounted display, and report its measured video delay and its use in one clinical case. Methods: The stereoscopic output of a 4K three-dimensional (3D) exoscope and the intraoperative computed tomography (CT) navigation display were streamed over a dedicated local network to an Apple Vision Pro, together with four locally rendered reference layers; the exoscopic image was delivered at 1920 × 1080 in side-by-side stereoscopic format, that is, 960 × 1080 per eye. The delay of each streamed image relative to its native display was measured at the mirrored output with a 240-frames/s high-speed camera. The system was used during exoscopic minimally invasive open-door laminoplasty through a 3-cm incision for multilevel cervical ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament. Results: The head-mounted exoscopic image lagged the native monitor by 30.8 ± 2.3 ms (range, 29.2-33.3 ms; n = 5), and the navigation image by 49.2 ± 1.9 ms (range, 45.8-50.0 ms; n = 5). The headset was worn for approximately 100 min without adjustment, malfunction, or reversion to the fallback monitor, and the procedure was completed without complication. Conclusions: The configuration was technically feasible with a small, measured delay. No ergonomic, workload, or clinical benefit is claimed.

title: Deep Learning Reconstruction for High-b-Value FOCUS DWI in Pancreatic Cancer: Image Quality Improvement and Effects on ADC Measurements.
abstract: Objectives: To evaluate whether deep learning reconstruction (DLR) improves pancreas-referenced image quality in high-b-value field-of-view optimized and constrained undistorted single-shot diffusion-weighted imaging (FOCUS DWI) for pancreatic cancer, and to assess reconstruction-related changes in apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) measurements in tumor and non-tumorous pancreatic regions. Methods: This prospective single-center study included 68 patients with pathologically confirmed pancreatic cancer who underwent 3.0-T pancreatic MRI. FOCUS DWI was acquired with b values of 0, 1000, 1500, and 2000 s/mm 2 and reconstructed with and without DLR. Quantitative metrics included lesion signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), lesion-to-pancreas contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), lesion-to-pancreas signal intensity ratio (LP-SIR), and ADC values in tumor regions and non-tumorous pancreatic parenchyma. Two abdominal radiologists independently assessed composite image quality and lesion conspicuity using a 5-point ordinal scale. Paired comparisons were performed with Holm correction across b values. Results: DLR significantly increased lesion SNR and lesion-to-pancreas CNR at b = 1000, 1500, and 2000 s/mm 2 (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Absolute image quality was highest at b = 1000 s/mm 2 , whereas the greatest DLR-related lesion SNR gain occurred at b = 1500 s/mm 2 . LP-SIR remained broadly stable after DLR (Holm-adjusted p = 0.767, 1.000, and 1.000). Tumor regions showed lower ADC values than non-tumorous pancreatic parenchyma across all b values and reconstruction conditions (all p < 0.001), while ADC values did not differ significantly between DLR and non-DLR reconstructions within either region ( p = 0.414-0.794). Qualitative scores improved after DLR for both readers at all b values (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), with weighted κ ranging from 0.717 to 0.896. Conclusions: DLR improved ROI-based quantitative image-quality metrics and qualitative image assessment in high-b-value pancreatic FOCUS DWI, with the greatest lesion SNR gain at b = 1500 s/mm 2 . No statistically significant reconstruction-related differences in ADC measurements were observed within tumor or non-tumorous pancreatic regions.

title: Patients Aged ≥65 Years with Metastatic Colon Cancer: Associations of Clinicopathological Factors, Skeletal Muscle Mass, and Inflammatory-Nutritional Indices with Survival.
abstract: Objective : Prognostic assessment in older patients with metastatic colon cancer remains challenging. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of clinicopathological characteristics, computed tomography (CT)-defined low skeletal muscle mass, and inflammatory-nutritional indices with overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Methods : This single-center study analyzed data from 141 patients aged ≥65 years who received first-line systemic therapy between 2020 and 2026. Skeletal muscle index was evaluated in 128 patients using pretreatment CT images. Survival outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis. Results : The median age was 71 years, and 75.0% of evaluable patients had a low skeletal muscle mass. The median OS was 30.32 months (95% confidence interval [CI]: 26.60-34.05), while the median PFS was 10.28 months (95% CI: 8.59-11.98). Synchronous metastases (hazard ratio [HR] = 3.745), Grade 3 tumors (HR = 3.084), absence of metastasectomy (HR = 3.650), high Köhne risk (HR = 2.546) and elevated carbonhydrate antigen [CA19-9] levels (HR = 1.812) were independently associated with shorter OS. Body mass index (BMI) of ≥25 kg/m 2 was associated with a lower risk of mortality (HR = 0.624). High Köhne risk (HR = 2.162), Grade 3 tumors (HR = 1.750), elevated carcinoembryonic antigen [CEA] levels (HR = 1.716) and elevated CA19-9 levels (HR = 1.579) were independently associated with shorter PFS. No statistically significant difference was found between low skeletal muscle mass and survival. Furthermore, none of the inflammatory-nutritional indices included in the key multivariable models maintained their independent prognostic significance. Conclusions : High Köhne risk, poor tumor differentiation, and elevated CA19-9 levels were independently associated with shorter OS and PFS in older patients with metastatic colon cancer. There was no statistically significant difference between low skeletal muscle mass and survival outcomes, while inflammatory-nutritional indices did not show independent prognostic significance in the key multivariable models. Further prospective studies involving larger patient populations are needed to confirm these results.

title: The Modern Era for Distal Radius Fragility Fracture Management: A Comprehensive Narrative Review on Current Guidelines and Unresolved Controversies.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Distal radius fractures (DRFs) are highly prevalent injuries, particularly in the aging demographic. Their management is currently undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift away from a strict focus on generic radiographic alignment toward personalized, functional recovery. Furthermore, in the geriatric population, a DRF is no longer viewed merely as an isolated orthopaedic injury, but as a critical sentinel event indicating systemic skeletal fragility. Previous consensus statements and reviews have left critical controversies unresolved, presenting conflicting guidelines regarding surgical indications, instability prediction, and rehabilitation. The purpose of this review is to explicitly identify these historical controversies, provide evidence-graded recommendations, and highlight translational innovations specifically for the older adult demographic. Methods : This current concepts review synthesizes the recent literature to provide an evidence-based update on the continuum of care for DRFs. Clinical recommendations were established through collaborative review and synthesis by a panel of orthopaedic surgeons that focus on orthopaedic trauma and/or hand surgery. Results : The classic Lafontaine criteria for predicting instability have shown unacceptable discriminative performance, prompting innovative adoption of integrated and machine learning (ML) predictive models utilizing pre- and post-reduction parameters. Whilst previous consensus had controversy on surgical thresholds in the elderly, the recent literature presents a nuanced debate; although some network meta-analyses suggest superior functional scores with surgical fixation, robust evidence confirms that for low-demand, physiologically older patients, these differences are rarely clinically significant, making conservative management a highly viable option. Older patients also face a high imminent risk of secondary fractures following a DRF, and orthogeriatric co-management via a Fracture Liaison Service (FLS) is becoming a vital translational solution. Economically, DRF operative care has also shifted toward ambulatory pathways, primarily utilizing regional blocks with sedation in North America, alongside the emerging alternative of Wide-Awake Local Anaesthesia No Tourniquet (WALANT) for highly selected fracture patterns. To mitigate operative complications, the use of intraoperative safety checklist can be a useful adjunct. Emerging technologies including AI-guided robotic-assisted reduction systems offer experimental promise in enhancing surgical precision. Postoperatively, wearable biofeedback sensors optimize functional rehabilitation, and novel biological adjuncts such as low-magnitude high-frequency vibration (LMHFV) and Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP), and dual-drug (testosterone/alendronate) coated membranes are being explored to enhance osteoporotic fracture healing. Conclusions : The innovation of this review lies in redefining DRF management through a patient-specific and risk-stratified approach. By resolving past controversies, we recommend a translated continuum of care that emphasizes secondary fracture prevention through FLS pathways, AI-integrated instability prediction, activity-demand treatment thresholds, ambulatory care alternatives, intraoperative safety checklists, experimental robotic-assisted precision, technology-assisted rehabilitation, biological enhancement of fracture healing.

title: Impact of Selected Cardiac Disorders on Retinal Microcirculation and Choroidal Thickness Assessed by Optical Coherence Tomography and OCT Angiography: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Aim: To summarise the impact of cardiovascular diseases on retinal and choroidal microcirculation assessed by optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography (OCTA) in patients with heart failure, myocardial infarction and atrial fibrillation, and to evaluate whether potential microvascular changes detected by OCTA depend on haemodynamic status or treatment. Methods: Published original studies investigating retinal microcirculation using OCTA and choroidal thickness using OCT in patients with selected cardiovascular diseases were reviewed. The analysed OCTA parameters included vessel density in the superficial and deep capillary plexuses, radial peripapillary capillaries, and macular regions, as well as the foveal avascular zone. Subfoveal and central choroidal thickness measurements were considered separately. Associations with cardiac function, haemodynamic status, and treatment-related changes were also reviewed. Results: In patients with heart failure, reduced retinal vessel density was frequently observed. Some studies reported associations between New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, left ventricular ejection fraction, and retinal microvascular changes. Reduced choroidal thickness was reported in several heart failure studies. In patients with acute decompensated heart failure, perfusion parameters improved following clinical recompensation. Findings in patients with myocardial infarction were inconsistent: while some studies reported no significant differences in retinal vessel density or foveal avascular zone measurements, others demonstrated reduced microvascular density. In patients with atrial fibrillation, decreased flow density in the superficial capillary plexus was reported. Selected studies also demonstrated improvements in certain retinal microvascular parameters and choroidal thickness following interventional procedures. Recent studies described FAZ enlargement and choroidal thinning in HFpEF, and potential associations of deep parafoveal vessel density and choroidal thickness with coronary risk scores in NSTEMI. Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that cardiovascular diseases may be associated with retinal microvascular alterations detectable by OCTA. The most consistent findings concern heart failure and atrial fibrillation, whereas results in patients with myocardial infarction remain inconclusive. OCTA may represent a promising non-invasive tool for investigating microvascular changes associated with cardiovascular disease and exploring treatment-associated microvascular changes; diagnostic and prognostic applications require prospective validation.

title: High-Strength Deep Learning Image Reconstruction Versus Adaptive Statistical Iterative Reconstruction for Stenosis Assessment in Stented Coronary Vessels on Coronary CT Angiography: A Multireader Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: To compare high-strength deep learning image reconstruction (DLIR-H) with adaptive statistical iterative reconstruction (ASIR-V) for coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) of stented vessels, evaluating image quality, stenosis measurement accuracy, and classification performance against invasive coronary angiography (ICA) as reference standard. Methods: This retrospective single-centre study included 20 patients (30 coronary vessels) with prior stent implantation and ≥50% stenosis on CCTA. Datasets were reconstructed using ASIR-V and DLIR-H. Four blinded readers assessed subjective image quality and in-stent lumen and vessel stenosis degree; Bayesian hierarchical models accounted for reader and vessel variability. Results: DLIR-H improved subjective noise ratings (posterior probability >99%) and reduced in-stent lumen stenosis measurement error by approximately 15% (estimate: -0.16; 90% credible interval: -0.30 to -0.01; probability: 96%), with no clear evidence of an effect on native-vessel stenosis measurement error (probability: 72%). False-positive stent-level classifications (CAD-RADS ≥4) decreased from 10 to 4 reader assessments, whereas false-negative classifications increased from 2 to 4. Only one stent was reference-positive on ICA. Inter-reader agreement was similar for both reconstructions. Conclusions: In this exploratory study, DLIR-H was associated with a modest reduction in in-stent lumen stenosis measurement error, with no benefit for native vessel stenosis. At the stent level, DLIR-H shifted classifications towards CAD-RADS ≤3 but did not improve classification accuracy. Inter-reader agreement was limited with both reconstructions. Given the small sample and the single stent with ≥70% stenosis on ICA, these findings should be regarded as preliminary and require confirmation before informing routine clinical use.

title: Comparative Accuracy of a Commercial Multimodal Large Language Model Versus Clinicians in Dental Age and Sex Estimation from Panoramic Radiographs: A Benchmark Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Routine dental imaging captures cumulative dentoalveolar and periodontal changes, offering a non-invasive window into both chronological aging and physiological senescence. While task-specific deep learning models have been widely explored in dental radiology, the zero-shot diagnostic performance of commercial Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in adult populations remains underinvestigated. The aim of this study was to benchmark the zero-shot diagnostic accuracy and repeatability of a commercial MLLM against human clinicians of varying experience levels in estimating adult dental age and biological sex from panoramic radiographs (OPGs), using documented chronological age and biological sex as the ground truth. Methods: From 216 initially screened records, this retrospective single-center study included 127 standardized, anonymized OPGs from patients (74 men, 53 women; mean chronological age 55.5 ± 15.8 years, range 18-90 years) treated at the Clinical Department of Cranio-Maxillofacial Surgery, Military Institute of Medicine-National Research Institute in Warsaw. Each radiograph was independently evaluated across three trials by Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, Mountain View, CA, USA) and once by two clinicians-a maxillofacial specialist (>10 years of experience) and a resident (<3 years of experience)-all blinded to clinical metadata. Results: Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated excellent repeatability across the three trials (ICC(A,1) = 0.926, ICC(A,3) = 0.974; p = 0.156) and moderate agreement with chronological age (ICC(A,1) = 0.604), but systematically overestimated age by a mean of 6.23 years. Mean absolute error (MAE) ranged from 12.91 to 13.03 years across the AI trials. The specialist achieved a significantly lower MAE (10.39 years) than all AI assessments (adjusted p ≤ 0.003), whereas the resident (MAE = 11.19 years) did not differ significantly from the AI (adjusted p = 0.282). In biological sex classification the specialist (66.1%) significantly outperformed all three AI trials (41.7-49.6%), while the resident (62.2%) significantly outperformed the first two AI trials (41.7% and 43.3%), but did not differ significantly from the third trial (49.6%). Across all runs, the AI exhibited significant directional asymmetry ( p < 0.001), frequently misclassifying male patients as female. Conclusions: While Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated high internal repeatability and age-estimation accuracy comparable to a junior resident, its wide limits of agreement, systematic age overestimation, and poor sex-classification accuracy preclude its autonomous use in clinical or forensic workflows. Future studies incorporating healthy control cohorts and validated clinical indices are required to determine whether the observed age overestimation reflects inherent algorithmic miscalibration or sensitivity to cumulative dentoalveolar pathology in hospitalized patients.

title: Artificial Intelligence Across the Scoliosis Surgical Pathway: A Structured Narrative Review of Preoperative Planning, Instrumentation Support, and Postoperative Assessment.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly investigated in scoliosis surgery, but its clinical readiness varies across applications. This structured narrative review examines AI applications across preoperative planning, intraoperative support, and postoperative assessment, focusing on methodological limitations, validation, and clinical utility. Methods : English-language publications were identified iteratively through PubMed and reference-list screening during approximately one year of manuscript preparation. The adopted publication window was 1 January 2022, to 27 August 2026. A.F. and R.K. selected and reviewed the literature. Twenty-two distinct primary studies were organized by clinical task and synthesized narratively. Qualitative appraisal was informed by PROBAST + AI, QUADAS-2, ROBINS-I, CLAIM, and relevant reporting guidelines; formal tool-based risk-of-bias ratings and quantitative pooling were not undertaken. PRISMA-ScR was not applied because this work was designed as a structured narrative review. Results : Preoperative applications included fusion-level selection, prediction of postoperative alignment, and risk stratification. Specialized systems demonstrated promising performance, including external validation, whereas general-purpose multimodal language models showed inconsistent agreement with expert surgical decisions. Applications informing intraoperative care primarily involved pedicle screw trajectory planning and patient-specific rod geometry rather than real-time adaptive guidance. Postoperative applications encompassed automated alignment measurements, instrumentation classification, implant monitoring, and complication prediction. A multicentre radiographic system achieved a mean absolute error of 2.7° for major-curve measurement, while selected growing-rod and vertebral body tethering studies reported measurement errors below 1 mm and 1°, respectively. However, evidence was frequently limited by small retrospective cohorts, insufficient external validation, incomplete calibration assessment, and limited evaluation of clinical impact. Mixed adult spinal deformity cohorts provided indirect evidence and were distinguished from scoliosis-specific populations. Conclusions : AI shows promise for automating defined imaging tasks and supporting individualized scoliosis surgical planning and follow-up. Technical accuracy alone does not establish clinical benefit. Prospective multicentre validation, transparent reporting, and evaluation of effects on decisions, complications, reoperations, and patient-reported outcomes are needed before routine implementation.

title: Conventional Versus Three-Dimensional Planning and Computer-Assisted Surgery for Limb and Pelvic Structural Allograft Reconstruction After Musculoskeletal Tumour Resection: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Comparative evidence for three-dimensional (3D) planning and computer-assisted surgery (CAS) in structural allograft reconstruction is limited. We examined associations with function and radiographic integration. Methods: This retrospective single-centre cohort included 49 patients undergoing musculoskeletal tumour resection: 37 underwent conventional and 12 CAS-assisted reconstruction. Co-primary outcomes were final Musculoskeletal Tumor Society (MSTS) and International Society of Limb Salvage (ISOLS) scores. Regression adjusted for surgical era and case mix; sensitivity analysis included 32 patients treated from 2018 onward. Results: CAS-assisted reconstruction was associated with higher MSTS (25.7 versus 21.5; difference 4.18, 95% CI 1.47-6.89; Hedges g = 0.92; p = 0.004) and ISOLS (21.5 versus 17.2; difference 4.26, 95% CI 2.21-6.30; g = 1.01; p < 0.001). Adjusted coefficients in the 32-patient contemporary-cohort sensitivity model were 7.52 for MSTS (95% CI 4.45-10.60) and 5.46 for ISOLS (95% CI 2.26-8.66). Each ISOLS point was associated with 0.53 MSTS points (95% CI 0.21-0.84). Union and complication comparisons were inconclusive. Conclusions: CAS-assisted reconstruction was associated with concordantly better functional and radiographic outcomes. These observational findings support prospective evaluation but do not establish causality.

title: Do Saliency Maps Look Where a Human Annotator Looks? An Exploratory Gaze-Based Benchmark of Explainable AI for Colonoscopic Polyp Segmentation.
abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) maps are often judged by whether they highlight what a human would look at, but this is rarely tested against recorded eye movements. This exploratory benchmark compared the fixations of a single annotator from the open GazeMedSeg dataset (26,832 fixations on 1000 Kvasir-SEG colonoscopy images, recorded while the annotator located and then scanned a polyp present in every image) with seven attribution methods for three polyp segmentation U-Nets (test Dice 0.829 ± 0.004). The first fixation fell on the polyp in 45% of images and the second in 93% of images, and 85-91% of fixations in each later fixation-order group fell inside it. Over the whole image, decoder-layer Grad-CAM agreed best with gaze among the explanations (correlation 0.62; 0.65 at matched resolution), yet the model's own probability map agreed slightly better (paired difference -0.023, 95% CI -0.032 to -0.013). Inside the lesion, no method showed statistically significant positive residual agreement with gaze after the tested geometry controls. The most faithful methods in deletion-insertion tests (GradientSHAP, Integrated Gradients) were among the least aligned with gaze, but the faithfulness ranking depended on the test protocol, and gradient-based maps failed a model-randomisation check. Gaze-based evaluation of segmentation explanations therefore needs a model-output baseline, resolution-matched maps and geometry-controlled within-lesion analysis; the findings are specific to one annotator, task-directed viewing and one architecture.

title: Deep Learning-Based Classification of Root Fusion Morphology in Maxillary Second Molars on Cone-Beam Computed Tomography: Impact of Image Preprocessing.
abstract: Maxillary second molars with root fusion exhibit considerable anatomical variability that complicates dental treatment planning. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) has become an essential imaging modality for evaluating such complex morphology. This study aimed to develop a deep learning (DL)-based computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) system for the automated classification of root fusion types in maxillary second molars, and to systematically evaluate the impact of image preprocessing strategies on model performance. CBCT images from 172 maxillary second molars (3188 two-dimensional slices) were collected and classified into seven root fusion types. A ResNet50 convolutional neural network was trained with tooth-level 5-fold cross-validation. The effects of grayscale bit depth (4096 vs. 256 levels), preprocessing mode (original, binarized, and segmented images), and contrast enhancement techniques (histogram equalization [HE] and contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization [CLAHE] with varying parameters) on classification accuracy were systematically compared. The model trained on segmented, non-binarized images with 4096 grayscale levels achieved the highest overall accuracy of 91.6%. In descending order of performance: CLAHE-1 (90.5%), CLAHE-3 (90.5%), CLAHE-40 (88.2%), and HE (83.9%). The unprocessed original image group yielded the lowest accuracy (57.5%). A ResNet50-based DL system can effectively classify complex root fusion morphology in maxillary second molars. Preserving the natural radiopacity gradient of CBCT images, rather than applying artificial contrast enhancement, was critical for optimal model performance. These findings provide a reference for preprocessing strategy selection in dental CBCT-based AI systems.

title: Intraoperative Radiographic Visualization of the Schneiderian Membrane Using the Novel Hydraulic Contrast Lift Protocol: A Retrospective Clinical Case Series.
abstract: Background: Limited intraoperative visibility during transcrestal sinus floor elevation complicates assessment of membrane elevation and possible perforation before graft placement. This retrospective case series evaluated the clinical feasibility and preliminary clinical and radiographic outcomes of the Hydraulic Contrast Lift (HCL) protocol. Materials and methods: A retrospective case series was conducted on seven patients treated with the HCL protocol. The technique uses a hydraulic delivery system to inject a radiopaque contrast medium beneath the Schneiderian membrane. Primary procedural endpoints were membrane visualization and controlled elevation without radiographic signs of perforation. Clinical endpoints included integration of the bone substitute, implant osseointegration, and implant survival. Bone height changes were assessed using preoperative cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and post-healing periapical radiographs or CBCT. Results: Successful intraoperative membrane visualization was achieved in all seven cases (100%), with no radiographic evidence of Schneiderian membrane perforation. The mean preoperative residual bone height was 4.5 ± 2.0 mm (range: 1.5-8 mm), and the mean postoperative bone height gain was 9.0 ± 3.3 mm (range: 4-12 mm). Five patients (71.4%) received simultaneous implant placement and two (28.6%) underwent delayed placement. All grafted areas showed radiographic continuity with adjacent bone, and all implants achieved successful osseointegration. Implant survival after implant loading (9-47 months; mean: 28.1 ± 12.8 months) was 100%. Conclusions: Within the limitations of this small retrospective case series, the HCL protocol appeared feasible, enabling intraoperative radiographic visualization of the sinus membrane and controlled elevation. No radiographic signs of membrane perforation or clinical complications were observed. Radiographic bone height gain and favorable implant outcomes were documented during follow-up. Larger prospective studies are needed to evaluate safety, reproducibility, and long-term clinical outcomes.

title: SSGNet++: Stage-Aware Generative Augmentation and Ensemble-Guided Pseudo-Labelling for Medical Imaging.
abstract: Limited annotation and class imbalance remain important challenges in medical image analysis. SSGNet++ examines class-specific StyleGAN3 augmentation for classification and an iterative pseudo-labelling pipeline for segmentation, combining predictions from heterogeneous multi-base and multi-head models with optional mask refinement. We evaluate four classification tasks and four segmentation tasks drawn from six public datasets. In the classification experiments, the best tested synthetic-data settings increased accuracy by 3-7 percentage points over real-only training in several dataset settings, although the preferred augmentation ratio varied and larger ratios could reduce performance. The initial segmentation analyses examined single models, ensembles, iterative pseudo-label training, and refinement stages, but reused validation partitions for both model selection and performance reporting; these results are, therefore, exploratory and may be optimistic. Four-seed follow-ups comprised a post-hoc internal split (112 runs) and a partial external-cohort evaluation (64 runs); multi-head gains were uncertain and refinement effects varied by dataset. These follow-ups remain limited by the post-hoc internal split and incomplete external comparisons.

title: DCLCA-UNet: Dynamic Cross-Level Contextual Attention for 3D Medical Image Segmentation.
abstract: Accurate 3D medical image segmentation requires effective integration of encoder details and decoder semantics. However, their relative contributions vary across decoding stages and spatial locations, and attention based only on the current feature pair may provide limited guidance in ambiguous regions. To address these challenges, we propose Dynamic Cross-Level Contextual Attention U-Net (DCLCA-UNet), which reconstructs cross-level context at each decoding stage from the incoming decoder feature and encoder features at the corresponding and shallower levels. The Cross-Level Contextual Attention Fusion (CLCAF) module uses this context to adaptively weight encoder and decoder features before fusion. The Context-Guided Feature Modulation (CGFM) module then reuses the context to refine the fused representation through scaling and additive correction. Experiments on Synapse, BTCV, and BraTS2023 yield average Dice scores of 88.70%, 84.13%, and 92.34%, respectively, with the lowest corresponding average Hausdorff distance (HD) or 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) among the compared methods. These improvements are accompanied by increased computational cost. Repeated experiments and evaluation on AMOS22 provide additional evidence of stability and cross-dataset generalization. Ablation studies further assess the contributions of contextual fusion, modulation, and stage-specific context reconstruction. Together, these results support the effectiveness of contextual guidance in volumetric segmentation.

title: Annotation-Free Vision-Language Concept Bottleneck Models for Interpretable Medical Image Classification: A Review.
abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) route predictions through a layer of human-understandable concepts, but classical CBMs need a concept label for every training image, a cost that is high in medicine. Vision-language models (VLMs) remove that requirement because, in a shared image-text embedding space, a large language model can propose candidate concepts and contrastive similarity can score them, with no concept labels. This review surveys annotation-free VLM-based CBMs and their move into clinical imaging. We cover vision-language foundations (CLIP, ALIGN, LLaVA) and trace concept models from early supervised methods (CBM, CEM, TCAV) to versions that work without manual labels (LaBo, Label-Free CBM, PCBM, OpenCBM, VLG-CBM). We then map these foundations to specific medical fields such as radiology, pathology, cardiology, dermatology, and ophthalmology, highlighting the medical VLM-CBMs closest to actual deployment (CBVLM, AdaCBM, ConcepPath, CBM-RAG). We focus on information leakage, in which task information reaches the prediction through the concept layer without being carried by the named concepts. Two of the seven surveyed medical VLM-CBMs test whether their predictions depend on individual concepts, but none measures leakage, and no shared protocol exists. We identify this gap as a central challenge for interpretable medical AI.

title: AI-Assisted Sequential Graf Assessment of Infant Hip Ultrasound: A Retrospective Single-Centre Evaluation in a Referral Cohort.
abstract: Graf-method ultrasound supports early assessment of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). This study assessed a sequential artificial-intelligence-assisted workflow and clinicians' Checklist I decisions with and without computer-aided diagnosis (CAD). This retrospective single-centre study of referred infants used 1803 development images from 679 examinations and separate cohorts of 1024 workflow and 100 reader images; Graf IV hips were excluded. ResTransUNet segmented eight Checklist I structures to assess reportability. Fifteen clinicians assessed the reader images unaided and four weeks later with CAD. Stand-alone Checklist I accuracy was 93.0% (93/100; 95% CI 86.3-96.6). Of 1024 workflow images, 846 received final outputs; Checklist II non-compliance precision was 48.1%. Among accepted images, the non-type-I endpoint had 81.0% accuracy, 82.7% sensitivity and 80.4% specificity; exact Graf-type agreement was 40.1%. Across entering non-type-I images, 167/266 (62.8%) received a correct positive output. Mean absolute errors were 3.59° for the α angle and 11.91° for the β angle, with a β-angle bias of +11.07°. Clinician accuracy was 72.3% unaided and 90.2% assisted-an observed 17.9 percentage-point difference (95% CI 10.0-26.1); 26 correct decisions became incorrect on AI-error cases. The workflow supported Checklist I assessment, but fixed order precludes causal CAD inference; gate failures and angle errors require refinement and prospective evaluation before clinical implementation.

title: Efficient Parallel Implementation of a 3-D MRF-Based Deformable Image Registration Algorithm in Medical Dynamic CT Imaging.
abstract: Registration techniques play a critical role in computer vision and medical image analysis, enabling the alignment of images acquired at different times or from different modalities. The increasing demand for high-resolution and real-time processing necessitates faster deformable registration algorithms; however, many accurate methods remain computationally expensive, limiting their clinical applicability. This work presents three acceleration strategies for a 3D MRF-based deformable image registration algorithm applied to dynamic CT imaging. First, the parallelizable components of the algorithm were identified and parallelized on the CPU using OpenMP. Second, a fully GPU-based implementation using CUDA was developed. Third, a heterogeneous hybrid CPU/GPU implementation was designed to optimally distribute computational tasks across both platforms. Experimental results on the Learn2Reg dataset with images of size (192 × 160 × 256), demonstrate that the hybrid approach achieves the best overall performance by strategically offloading sequential graph-based bottlenecks to the CPU. It achieves a speedup factor of ~9× compared to the Serial implementation while maintaining comparable accuracy, overcoming the severe hardware utilization limits of the fully GPU-based approach and highlighting the challenges of mapping MRF optimization to massively parallel architectures. These results indicate that hybrid computing architectures provide an effective trade-off between computational efficiency and registration accuracy. A graphical user interface was also developed to visualize the registration process and results.

title: Improving Accuracy and Evaluating the Generalizability of Medical Image Classification Using Pseudo-Invisible-Light Images Generated from RGB Images.
abstract: We extend our previous study on extended 5-channel images, which add two pseudo-invisible-light channels, estimated by spectral reconstruction (MST++) and polynomial extrapolation, to the RGB channels. We first ask whether the accuracy gain reflects prior knowledge contributed by the externally trained spectral-reconstruction model or effects that any 5-channel input derived from RGB would produce. For skin cancer classification with a CNN trained from scratch, the proposed input is compared with grayscale-based extensions, duplicated RGB channels, learned pointwise transforms of RGB, and learned projections of the reconstructed spectrum. Duplicating RGB channels alone raised accuracy from 86.49% to 88.27%; learned transforms of RGB did not significantly exceed this level, whereas the proposed input (89.94%) exceeded both; learned projections of the reconstructed spectrum did not differ significantly from it. We then re-evaluate the method on diabetic retinopathy, gastrointestinal, and glaucoma classification with ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50, with wavelengths selected on validation data. The proposed input exceeded RGB by 1.5-2.1 percentage points in all three tasks, as did most wavelength combinations, but these gains were not significant and not distinguishable from the RGB-duplication control; an effect specific to the proposed input remains unestablished there. Computational cost is also reported.

title: Refining Retinal Vessel Segmentation with Conditional Diffusion Models: A Controlled Evaluation on LU-Net+RA Probability Maps.
abstract: Retinal vessel segmentation remains difficult along thin, low-contrast branches. We evaluate a conditional diffusion refiner for probability maps from a lightweight U-Net with reverse attention (LU-Net+RA). A frozen mask autoencoder produces a spatially downsampled multi-channel grid; a global RGB embedding conditions denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) updates, followed by frozen decoding. The refiner adds 527,233 parameters to the 1,946,961-parameter backbone. Matched evaluation on CHASE-DB1, DRIVE and HRF uses five training seeds and five sampling seeds. Refined mean Dice was 0.746, 0.790 and 0.666, against coarse values of 0.811, 0.792 and 0.732. Exploratory paired intervals exclude zero in the negative direction. Conditioning variants changed Dice by less than 0.0002. Deterministic encoded-grid refinement and autoencoder fine-tuning narrowed the gap but exceeded the baseline only on DRIVE; spatial residual refinement changed Dice by -0.0001, +0.0058 and +0.0074. Matched out-of-fold training did not establish absence of input shift. Increasing DDIM updates from 50 to 100 doubled refinement time with negligible observed Dice change. An earlier single-run result was not reproduced. Under this controlled protocol, diffusion refinement did not improve LU-Net+RA.

title: Binding Text to Pixels: A Narrative Review of Supervision Granularity in Language-Guided Chest Radiograph Segmentation and Grounding.
abstract: Chest radiographs come with abundant free-text reports but scarce lesion-level annotation, so report text increasingly supervises localization. This structured narrative review, written for model developers, benchmark curators, and evaluators of clinical AI, covers phrase grounding, weakly supervised localization, language-guided segmentation, grounded report generation, and multimodal large language models to September 2026. We propose a five-level granularity ladder, organizing the field by where text binds to the image, not by architecture, as an explanatory framework and testable hypothesis, and show that separating train-time binding from inference-time output exposes the most informative systems. A resource audit classifying each corpus's spatial signal as reader-drawn, image-derived, or report-derived reveals a structural gap: at MIMIC-CXR scale, lesion masks exist only when generated from the reports that supervise the models, and independent reader-drawn masks for multiple lesion types cover 234-902 images, roughly 400 to 1600 times fewer. On the shared MS-CXR benchmark, three studies report one model at 21.5 to 26.6 mean intersection over union, a spread exceeding most between-method differences. Grounded outputs are intended to make AI assertions checkable at the point of care, though prospective evidence is lacking. We specify an anatomy-referenced evaluation, propose federated subgroup evaluation, and recommend reserving reader-drawn masks for evaluation.

title: Survival Prediction from Public Brain Metastasis MRI Cohorts: A Positive-Control and Permutation-Based Feasibility Evaluation.
abstract: Public brain metastasis MRI cohorts are widely used for prognostic modeling, but whether an endpoint is identifiable at the available sample size is rarely tested. We evaluated eight clinical endpoints in two public cohorts, Yale/BraTS-MET (199 patients, 74 deaths) and OpenBTAI/MOLAB (75 patients, all deceased), using lesion-centered nnU-Net encoder embeddings and PyRadiomics features with patient-grouped cross-validation and label permutation. Patient-level infratentorial involvement served as a positive control (balanced accuracy 0.60); the Graded Prognostic Assessment (GPA) score was recoverable from OpenBTAI radiomics (ρ = 0.42), whereas brain age was not recovered in either cohort. Primary tumor type was the only endpoint significant after multiplicity correction (1.3× chance). Survival endpoints were null for clinical models and the planned graph model (C = 0.50, p = 0.49); an exploratory linear model on embeddings reached C ≈ 0.58 ( p = 0.07, uncorrected), which PyRadiomics features did not reproduce. No progression definition remained significant after family-wise correction. In simulation, 80% power required a true C-index of about 0.68-0.76, so null survival results cannot exclude moderate effects. GPA did not stratify survival ( p = 0.18) in a cohort containing only deceased patients. An extraction error found during revision was corrected.

title: Metric Positional Encoding in Transformer-Based 3D Medical Image Segmentation Under Controlled Spacing Changes.
abstract: In 3D computed tomography segmentation, differences in voxel spacing mean that equal separations on the voxel grid correspond to different physical distances. Many Transformers incorporate positional encodings because self-attention does not explicitly represent position. However, index-based encodings do not express these distances. Whether metric coordinates improve performance or the response to resampling remains unclear. We evaluated this effect using a factorial UNETR design that combined index or physical coordinates with additive Fourier encoding or 3D RoPE. In KiTS23, we evaluated 391 patients across three folds; 117 were resampled to inter-slice spacings of 3, 4, and 5 mm. Control conditions varied the supplied spacing without altering the image. We repeated the RoPE comparison after training the models from scratch on AMOS22-CT. Among the 117 eligible KiTS23 cases, the metric variants responded to the supplied spacing, but no average advantage in Surface Dice change after resampling was demonstrated (contrast: -0.0029; 95% CI: -0.0104 to 0.0043). In 38 eligible AMOS22-CT cases, metric RoPE maintained higher absolute Surface Dice than index-based RoPE, although its advantage decreased from 0.0512 at the original spacing to 0.0216 at 5 mm. The change in Surface Dice from the original-spacing condition was less favorable for metric RoPE (contrast: -0.0241; 95% CI: -0.0296 to -0.0186). For the evaluated models, metric coordinates did not demonstrate a more favorable response to retrospective resampling, despite sensitivity to supplied spacing and higher absolute Surface Dice in AMOS22-CT. The 95% confidence intervals quantify uncertainty due to patient sampling conditional on the trained models; they do not capture variability across training runs.

title: ImageBR: A Public MRI Dataset for Planned Implant Region and Mammary Gland Segmentation in Breast Reconstruction.
abstract: Breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers three-dimensional anatomical information for reconstruction-oriented analysis, but annotated public datasets targeting implant-based reconstruction are limited. ImageBR contains MRI volumes from 44 patients (26 bilateral and 18 unilateral reconstruction cases), yielding 70 breast-level samples with expert annotations of planned implant regions, mammary gland tissue, and breast regions. The planned implant region is a surgeon-defined virtual surgical target rather than a directly visible anatomical structure on MRI, and its reference annotations were established without using the final prosthesis specifications. A two-stage benchmark combines breast-region extraction with an nnU-Net 3D cascade incorporating image-derived anatomical priors and weighted loss optimization. Under patient-level three-fold cross-validation, the reported mean breast-level Dice scores were 83.0% and 74.4% for planned implant region and mammary gland segmentation, respectively. The retrospective comparison of predicted-region volume and diameter with final implanted prosthesis specifications yielded relative errors of 14.27% and 8.98%, respectively, and measures consistency rather than independent implant-selection accuracy.

title: Probability-Level Fusion of Meta-Information and Multimodal MRI/PET Radiomics for Predicting 1p/19q Codeletion and IDH Mutation in Gliomas.
abstract: Noninvasive prediction of 1p/19q codeletion and isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation may support preoperative assessment of lower-grade gliomas. We evaluated leakage-aware probability-level fusion of meta-information and multimodal radiomics. This retrospective study included 217 patients with World Health Organization grade II or III gliomas and preoperative magnetic resonance imaging and positron emission tomography. Meta-information and radiomics models were developed separately, and their calibrated probabilities were combined using weighted averaging or logit stacking. Performance was evaluated using repeated stratified five-fold nested cross-validation with 10 seeds, with all data-dependent procedures confined to training data. For 1p/19q codeletion, weighted averaging achieved an outer-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.816 ± 0.056 (mean ± standard deviation), and both fusion approaches achieved higher patient-level AUCs than meta-information alone after Holm correction. For IDH mutation, weighted averaging achieved an AUC of 0.799 ± 0.077 and a higher patient-level AUC than radiomics alone, whereas the comparison with meta-information alone was not statistically supported. Modality-group analyses revealed task-dependent performance patterns without identifying a consistently superior modality condition after multiplicity correction. Probability-level fusion showed task-dependent incremental discrimination and warrants further external and prospective evaluation with contemporary molecular reference standards and prespecified imaging harmonization procedures.

title: Beyond Segmentation: Coronary Artery Calcium Scoring with Frozen Self-Supervised CT Features.
abstract: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring on computed tomography (CT) acquired for other indications could provide calcium-burden information without a dedicated scoring examination. We investigate direct, segmentation-free Agatston score prediction from frozen CT patch representations using only volume-level supervision for the scoring head. A lightweight additive head maps attention-selected features to non-negative contributions, combines them within slices, and sums slice scores across each volume. In developmental evaluation, applying the nonlinear mapping before aggregation improved linearly weighted κ by 0.27-0.38 over a pooled multilayer perceptron across six encoders. Using spatially adaptive label-guided temperature (SALT) features, held-out κ was 0.930 on gated CT and 0.844 on contrast-enhanced coronary CT angiography (CCTA), with separately fitted heads. On external non-gated CT, a head fitted on 165 patients from the same cohort achieved κ=0.727 on 40 held-out patients; patient-level five-fold cross-validation over all 205 patients yielded κ=0.639, indicating preliminary local-adaptation performance. Unchanged-head external gated transfer achieved κ=0.854 (n=443). Gated intraclass correlation coefficient ICC(A,1) on log(1+score) was 0.984. Study-level CAC scores served as CCTA reference targets; non-contrast images were not model inputs. SALT uses gated calcium masks during pretraining, not downstream scoring. Its highest-attention patch overlapped calcium in 89.5% of calcium-bearing slices, but localization rankings did not directly track scoring rankings. These results support direct, spatially decomposable CAC prediction from reusable features; broader validation is needed before clinical use.

title: Fine-Coarse Dual Multi-Scale Graph Convolutional Network with Adaptive Edge Construction for Classification and Survival Prediction of Whole-Slide Images.
abstract: Whole-slide images (WSIs) provide important morphological evidence for cancer diagnosis and prognostic assessment. However, their gigapixel size, substantial regional heterogeneity, complex spatial organization, and limited fine-grained annotations make it difficult to model the topological relationships among pathological regions, which in turn limits the use of WSI analysis in automated diagnosis and prognosis. We propose AECGCN, a fine-coarse dual multi-scale graph convolutional network with adaptive edge construction, for WSI classification and survival prediction. Patch-level features are first extracted using the pretrained CONCH (CONtrastive learning from Captions for Histopathology) model and compressed by MiniBatch K-Means clustering to construct fine- and coarse-grained graphs. Graph edges are then constructed adaptively by combining spatial distance with feature-based semantic similarity, where the relative weighting is calibrated by Moran's I spatial autocorrelation statistic, so that tissue topology and pathological relationships are captured jointly. Finally, two task-specific subnets, AECGCN-C for classification and AECGCN-S for survival prediction, integrate local pathological patterns and global tissue structure through dual-branch graph convolutions and cross-scale attention. Evaluated on datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), AECGCN achieves classification accuracy (ACC) values of 0.944±0.024 on the combined kidney cohort (TCGA-Kidney) and 0.914±0.027 on the breast invasive carcinoma cohort (TCGA-BRCA). For survival prediction, it achieves concordance index (C-index) values of 0.709±0.041 on the kidney renal clear cell carcinoma cohort (TCGA-KIRC) and 0.644±0.043 on TCGA-BRCA. The study provides a research-stage framework for image-based subtype classification and prognostic risk stratification with exploratory attention visualization. External validation, probability calibration, prospective evaluation, and human-in-the-loop review remain necessary before clinical use. Because the framework relies only on slide-level labels and generic patch-level features, the same fine-coarse dual graph design with adaptive edge construction can be extended to other clinical imaging applications and to other multi-scale or gigapixel image analysis tasks.

title: Tumour-Guided Attention with Mask-Supervised Pooling for Leakage-Aware and Explainable Brain Tumour Classification in MRI: A Reproducibility and Evaluation Study.
abstract: Brain tumour classifiers are often reported as near-perfect and explainable without checking patient structure or annotations. We reproduced a recent attention framework (SSPANet) on the Figshare dataset (3064 T1-weighted contrast-enhanced slices, 233 patients). Its image-level split is fully patient-leaky; every configuration exceeds 98% accuracy, which drops by 5-9 points on the patient-wise split. Under a fixed training recipe, seven attention modules stayed within ±0.63 points of the plain backbone, whereas the recipe changed accuracy by up to 4.7 points. As a case study, TG-SSPANet uses expert masks to supervise attention, train a segmentation decoder and gate evidence pooling. With ResNet50, it reached 96.8% slice-level and, averaging slice probabilities, 98.3% patient-level accuracy (84.5% if every slice had to be correct; 15% of patients had discordant slices), within the confidence intervals of simpler mask-using pipelines; its attention module added no measurable benefit. Its Grad-CAM++ maps hit the tumour in 81% of held-out slices, but this follows from its decoder by construction, not the classifier's reasoning. After tumour inpainting, whole-slice models kept 80-86% accuracy, and shuffling the remaining tissue left 60-74%, so location, perilesional cues and tissue statistics cannot be separated. Patient-wise evaluation, same-recipe controls and mask-based faithfulness tests should precede explainability claims.

title: Chronic Hepatitis B and Steatotic Liver Disease: From Bidirectional Interaction to Hepatocellular Carcinoma Risk.
abstract: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) and steatotic liver disease (SLD) are among the most prevalent chronic liver diseases worldwide and increasingly coexist, particularly in regions where hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains endemic. Reported prevalence of hepatic steatosis in CHB varies widely, reflecting the diagnostic modality and population studied rather than a single underlying figure. Across series using liver biopsy, ultrasound or controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), hepatic steatosis in CHB is associated more consistently with host metabolic and genetic factors than with markers of viral replication. Hepatic steatosis is repeatedly associated with lower serum HBV DNA, lower quantitative hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), lower hepatitis B envelope antigen (HBeAg) positivity and a higher probability of HBsAg seroclearance. These virological associations do not consistently predict long-term liver outcomes, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk persists after HBsAg seroclearance. Studies using hepatic steatosis as the exposure report inconsistent findings for HCC, with adjusted estimates ranging from inverse to strongly positive. Metabolic dysfunction shows a more consistent association with HCC, particularly diabetes, obesity and multiple concurrent cardiometabolic risk factors, and this association persists in virologically suppressed patients and after HBsAg seroclearance. Hepatic steatosis, metabolic dysfunction, steatohepatitis and fibrosis should therefore be assessed as distinct prognostic variables rather than as a single entity, with implications for HCC risk stratification and surveillance in CHB.

title: Cross-Architecture Soft Voting for Cervical Vertebral Maturation Assessment from Lateral Cephalometric Radiographs.
abstract: Cervical vertebral maturation (CVM) assessment is clinically important for evaluating skeletal maturity in orthodontic treatment planning; however, manual staging is subjective and affected by inter-observer variability. This study presents a deep learning framework for six-class CVM classification from lateral cephalometric radiographs using architecture comparison, distribution-aware multi-task learning, prototype learning, and cross-architecture soft voting. The dataset consisted of 1749 radiographs from 1749 patients with CVM stage labels assigned by consensus of two oral and maxillofacial radiologists. MaxViT-Small, Swin-Base, ConvNeXt-Base, and EfficientNetV2-L were first evaluated using five-fold cross-validation under a CVM-only hard-label cross-entropy setting, and EfficientNetV2-L was used as the anchor backbone for a full factorial ablation of three components: Gaussian soft-label learning with Kullback-Leibler divergence, auxiliary sex prediction, and prototype learning. The components did not act independently: Gaussian soft labels improved class-balanced performance only when combined with the auxiliary sex task, and the complete formulation reached 77.82% accuracy, 60.89% Macro-F1, and 59.03% balanced accuracy, whereas the separate contribution of prototype learning could not be resolved at this sample size. The same final formulation was subsequently applied to four distinct backbones and combined using equal-weight cross-architecture soft voting. The ensemble achieved 79.82% accuracy (95% confidence interval 77.93-81.65%), 62.49% Macro-F1, 59.22% balanced accuracy, and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.908, with 97.77% of predictions within one stage of the reference. Relative to the best single model, the gains in accuracy and ordinal agreement were statistically supported, whereas those in Macro-F1 and balanced accuracy were not. An ensemble of independently trained models of a single backbone did not reproduce the accuracy gain, which is consistent with a benefit from architectural diversity; the necessity of all four members was not established. The gap of approximately 20 percentage points between overall and balanced accuracy reflects the predominance of CS6 (61.41%) and the low recall of the least represented early stages. All values are internal cross-validation estimates, and external validation is required before the framework can be considered for clinical use.
